feat(service map): collapse per-tenant fan-out, floor the row spacing

A project whose one instrumented service calls 149 third-party hosts rendered
every host as its own node. All 149 landed in one layer at a fixed 96px pitch —
~14,300px of virtual height — which fit-to-extent then crushed into a 456px box
at ~3px per row while symbols stayed 26-64px wide. The result was an unreadable
grey mass with a bundle of 150 identically-coloured edges attached.

Three changes, each with a guarantee rather than a heuristic:

Group. Uninstrumented host-shaped peers collapse by registrable domain
(eTLD+1), so 42 tenant subdomains become one `myshopify.com x42` node. Grouping
runs server-side before the node cap, so 150 slots now cover a whole fan-out
instead of 150 tenants. Both levels travel in the payload — a group's members
ride along with it — so expanding is a re-layout, not a second request. A group
of one is not a group. Databases never group; they are already named by system.

Floor. Row pitch stays generous while a layer fits, tightens to
rings-just-touching when it doesn't, and never goes below that: past the floor
the layer wraps into sub-columns instead. Fit-to-extent can no longer produce
spacing narrower than the nodes it spaces. The virtual extent also stops being
padded out to the container width, which was parking small graphs in the left
quarter of an empty canvas.

Quiet the edges. Neutral by default instead of coloured by source (in a fan-out
every edge shares one source, so that encoding said nothing while drowning the
red that means something). Width capped at 3px, failing edges painted last so
they sit on top, arrowheads dropped once the bundle is dense, and labels use
echarts' hideOverlap rather than overprinting into a grey mass.

A collapsed group's ring is red if ANY member is failing, and the tooltip says
"3 of 42 returning errors" — one endpoint at 100% inside 42 healthy ones is a
~2% aggregate, which is exactly the failure this map exists to surface.

Also replaces the literal NUL bytes used as the edge-key separator with a shared
`edgeKey` helper. The NULs made git treat the whole file as binary; this diff is
the last one that shows as Bin.

feat(service map): bound the map, fix the counts, grade health in three steps

Follow-up to the domain grouping, which fixed less than it looked like. The
real fan-out is not tenant subdomains of a few brands — it is hundreds of
unrelated merchant domains, one per customer. eTLD+1 grouping collapsed the one
genuine case (myshopify.com x71) and left ~160 singletons, so the map still drew
234 nodes.

Bound it. Datadog's map is bounded because it draws a query, not a universe.
We cannot filter a rollup by arbitrary predicates, but we can rank: keep the 12
busiest uninstrumented peers and fold the rest under the caller that reaches
them, as "N more dependencies". Folding is a second collapse level reusing the
same head/member shape as domain grouping, so heads nest — "225 more" opens into
"myshopify.com x71", which opens into its members — and the renderer still has
exactly one concept to expand. Collapse is a parameter, and the trace map passes
CollapseOff: hiding two of one request's five hops behind "3 more" would hide
precisely what that view exists to show.

Fix the counts. Collapsed members ride in the payload so expansion needs no
refetch, but they are not drawn, and the previous commit counted them: the
header claimed "234 services · 234 dependencies" for a map of 150, and the
dependency table listed both a group's aggregate row and all 71 member rows,
double-counting the same requests in a table people read during incidents. Every
count now goes through drawnNodes/drawnEdges, and a collapsed row says what it
stands for ("myshopify.com (71 endpoints)").

Grade health properly. `error_rate > 0` is not a health signal on an aggregate
view — across hundreds of third-party integrations essentially everything has
had one error in an hour, which is why the whole canvas went red and a genuinely
failing dependency became invisible. Three steps now: ok, elevated at 1%,
failing at 5%, applied to node rings, edges and the group tooltip.

Also turns autoCurveness back off. It spreads edges sharing a *pair*; in a fan
every edge has a different target, so it only bent 200 straight lines into arcs
across the whole canvas.

feat(service map): Datadog-style cards, 1:1 layout, scrolling canvas

The node was a hollow ring carrying one fact with the numbers hidden behind a
hover, so answering "which dependency is failing" meant hovering every node in
turn. Datadog's node is a card carrying four: name, error rate, latency and
throughput, all readable at a glance. This adopts that.

Each node is now a card built from echarts rich text — kind tag, name (with a
xN badge when it stands for a collapsed group), error rate graded in three
steps, p95 (or share of trace time on the trace map), a throughput chip and a
health bar. Volume is no longer encoded as node size: the req/s line states it
in numbers, which is both more precise and what lets every card be one size.

Three layout faults had to be fixed before cards could work, each found by
screenshotting the real page rather than by reasoning about the code:

- `layout:'none'` scales the supplied coordinates to fit the container,
  uniformly on both axes, so a merely *wide* graph was also squashed vertically
  and the pixel floor from the previous commit was silently undone — 86-unit
  rows arrived 40px apart and overlapped. The canvas is now sized to the graph
  and the viewport scrolls, so the fit is 1:1 by construction.
- `assignCoords` placed layer n at `n * X_GAP`, which assumes every layer is one
  column wide. A wrapped layer's second column landed 44px from the next layer's
  cards, which are 176px wide. The cursor now advances by how wide each layer
  actually got.
- SUBCOL_GAP was 45% of the layer gap — narrower than a card — so wrapping
  overlapped the very cards it was meant to make room for.

Also fixes `getChartStyles().tooltipBorderColor`, which read `--color-borderWeak`
— a token that has never existed. The empty string it returned made echarts fall
back to its own rotating palette, which is why every bordered chart mark came
out in chart colours instead of the neutral stroke; on the map it turned every
card border into a different colour and left health nothing to say. It is
`--color-strokeWeak`, and this affects chart tooltips app-wide.

The legend now teaches what the card cannot say for itself — solid vs dashed
border, and where the health thresholds sit — instead of shapes that no longer
exist, and it hides the service-colour row when there is only one swatch.

feat(service map): scope the map to one service, Datadog-style

Datadog's flow map answers a query, not "everything": its header reads "Showing
32 services from distributed traces matching this query" with the active scope
as a dismissable chip. We cannot answer an arbitrary predicate from a rollup —
there is no env or tag dimension in service_dependency_edges — but "this service
and everything it touches" is pure graph traversal, needs no schema change, and
is the scope people actually reach for mid-incident.

A node's menu now leads with "Focus on this service", which scopes the map to
that service's connected slice and re-lays it out. A Lucid-rendered chip states
the scope and the resulting count, and clears it. Scoping is applied before
collapsing, so expanding a group inside a scope cannot drag the rest of the
system back onto the canvas.

Two bugs found while verifying this in a real browser:

- The node menu lived inside the map container, which now scrolls, so it would
  have been clipped the moment a node sat near an edge. It is a sibling now.
- The menu's click listener had no abort signal and the selected node lived in a
  closure. `render` runs again whenever a hidden container gains a size, so a
  superseded render kept its listener and answered clicks with its own stale
  selection. The listener is signal-scoped and the selection lives on the menu
  element, which is the one shared thing all renders agree on.

fix(service map): highlight the hovered path instead of blacking out the map

Hovering a card dimmed every other card to 14% opacity and every other edge to
6%, leaving a near-blank canvas with one readable node on it. That is the
opposite of what the view is for: you hover a service in order to compare it
with its neighbours, and Datadog's map keeps them all fully legible while
drawing the hovered path in an accent.

echarts' `focus:'adjacency'` cannot express that. It styles only the item under
the cursor — a link's own `lineStyle` outranks the series-level emphasis, so the
adjacent hops kept their resting hairline grey — and everything it does not
focus goes through `blur`, which is the blackout. So the path is driven here
instead: `hovered` tracks the node under the cursor, and the edges incident to
it plus their endpoint cards are drawn in the brand accent at full opacity.
Nothing dims.

Hover restyles rather than rebuilds: a notMerge pass tears the series down and
takes the tooltip with it, so the card's numbers vanished on the very gesture
that was meant to show them. Node and link counts do not change on hover, so a
merge pass is both correct and what keeps the tooltip alive.

fix(service map): put the service colour back on the card

Card borders now belong to health, which left the "Service colors" legend row
describing a colour that appeared nowhere on the map. Datadog marks each node
with its service's own colour; this does the same with a chip on the name line,
so the legend documents something real again and a service is recognisable
across the map, the waterfall and the charts as PRODUCT.md intends.

echarts rich styles are per-series, so the colour arrives as a per-node `rich`
override merged onto a transparent series-level `svc` style.

feat(service map): label the lit path with its throughput

Datadog writes req/s on the highlighted hops, which is what turns "these are
connected" into "this is how much traffic actually flows". The label is declared
for every edge but its formatter returns empty off the lit path — a per-link
`label` override does not take on a graph series, and labelling all 53 edges at
once would bury the map it annotates.

feat(service map): flow top-down with real kind icons

Two of the three remaining differences from Datadog's request flow map.

Flow direction. Datadog reads top-down — entry points on the first row, each hop
a row further down — and that is what the eye expects from a "flow". The layout
axes swap: rows hold siblings, layers step down the page, and a row too wide for
the canvas wraps onto a sub-row instead of running off the side. The cursor
still advances by how tall each row actually got, so a wrapped row cannot land
in the next hop's lane.

Kind icons. The DB/EXT/QUEUE text tags become actual marks: a hexagon for an
instrumented service, a cylinder for a database, stacked layers for a queue, a
cloud for a third-party host, an arrow for an entry point. They are inline SVG
data URIs rather than our sprite sheet, which canvas cannot reach, and rather
than unicode glyphs, which render at the mercy of whatever font the OS
substitutes. Monochrome, so an icon never competes with health for attention.

feat(service map): environment facet, the last Datadog-parity gap

Datadog's flow map is scoped by a query, and its Env chip is the part of that
query we could not answer: service_dependency_edges had no environment
dimension, so "prod only" was unanswerable rather than merely unimplemented.

The span store already carries resource___deployment___environment___name, so
the rollup can group by it. Migration 0118 adds `env` and extends the primary
key to include it — prod and staging calling the same dependency are different
hops, and collapsing them would report one system's traffic as the other's. The
column defaults to '' rather than NULL because NULL is not comparable in a
primary key, which would let the same hop upsert twice and double every count.

The read path takes an optional environment and returns every environment seen
in the range, so the facet lists exactly what this project has reported rather
than a fixed guess. The facet is server-rendered links: environment is a rollup
dimension, so picking one is a new query, and a link survives reload and share
in a way client-side state does not. It hides itself entirely when nothing in
range reports an environment — a facet with no choices in it is furniture.

Existing rows keep '' and stay indistinguishable from genuinely unlabelled
traffic, which is the truthful outcome: we did not record their environment and
back-filling one would invent it.

test(service map): prove the env facet round-trips from span to rendered control

Ingests two environments, rolls them up, and asserts the facet's options, its
filtering, its empty case, and that the control actually renders — the path the
production migration exists to serve.

Revert "environment facet": it queried a column Postgres does not have

The Env facet was built on a false premise. `otel_logs_and_spans` in Postgres
defines nine resource columns and `resource___deployment___environment___name`
is not among them — that column belongs to the TimeFusion schema, and the
reference in Telemetry.hs is what misled me. The rollup's `useTf=False` path
reads Postgres, so the query was invalid there.

That one mistake accounts for every failure in the suite: not just the new env
round-trip test but all five pre-existing rollup tests, which run the same
query. They were green before this and are green again after.

Reverting rather than patching. Reading the environment out of the `resource`
JSONB would compile, but it has to be correct on TimeFusion as well as Postgres
and I cannot verify the TF side from here — shipping a second guess into the
same query would be the same error twice. The facet is worth having; it needs a
migration that adds the column to the span store, and a rollup change validated
against both stores, landed together with the code that reads it.

Note for whoever picks this up: migration 0118 has already been applied to the
production database and is NOT undone by this revert. Production still has the
seven-column primary key, which the deployed six-column ON CONFLICT cannot
match, so the service-map rollup cannot write until that PK is restored.

docs(service map): record why the Env facet is blocked, and the three findings

The column the obvious implementation reaches for does not exist in either
store; the environment is reachable from the nested resource JSON on both; and
the rollup's primary key cannot gain a column while the deployed ON CONFLICT
still names six. Written down because I made all three mistakes in order, and
the third one stopped production's rollup writing.

feat(service map): environment facet, via an additive table

Second attempt. The first widened service_dependency_edges' primary key, which
stopped the deployed six-column ON CONFLICT matching anything and took the
production rollup down with it.

Three things were wrong and are now settled:

- resource___deployment___environment___name exists in NEITHER store. Postgres
  declares nine resource___* columns; TimeFusion's schema was queried directly
  and has none either. The environment comes from the nested `resource` JSON,
  with the same precedence ProcessMessage uses. It is nested, not dot-keyed, so
  `resource->>'deployment.environment.name'` silently returns NULL rather than
  erroring, which is how the first attempt looked plausible.
- The environment must be part of the hop's identity, so it cannot simply be a
  column outside the key: two environments in one bucket become two rows with
  the same key in one INSERT, which Postgres rejects with "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
  command cannot affect row a second time". Not merely lossy — a hard error.
- It therefore cannot widen the existing key while the old code runs. A new
  table has neither problem: CREATE TABLE is inert to code that never names it,
  so schema and code can land in either order, which is the property the first
  attempt lacked.

The rollup writes both tables; the read prefers the env-dimensioned one per
bucket and falls back to the original for buckets rolled before this shipped, so
the map is never empty and no hop is counted twice. Dropping the original is the
contract half of expand/contract, once a full retention window has rolled.

test(service map): advance the clock before asserting the env facet renders

The handler's 1H window is relative to now and the read range is half-open, so a
bucket sitting exactly at now falls outside it — the graph came back empty and
the facet correctly hid itself. Same reason the page test advances the clock.

feat(service map): React Flow's architecture, without React or canvas

The map was an echarts `graph` series with every coordinate supplied by hand.
That put the node inside a bitmap, and everything awkward about this page
followed from it: cards could not use design tokens, so hex values were hand-fed
from getChartStyles (which is how a typo'd `--color-borderWeak` went unnoticed);
icons could not use the sprite sheet, so they became inline data URIs; tooltips
were HTML strings built in JS, which this codebase explicitly forbids; and the
canvas was inert to keyboard and screen readers.

None of what makes React Flow feel good is React. It is three plain layers: a
viewport that clips, one pane carrying a CSS transform, and DOM nodes above an
SVG edge layer. That is what this is now.

- Lucid owns the card markup, as a template the renderer clones per drawn node.
  Tokens, sprite icons, focus rings and `title` tooltips all work by default.
- Edges are SVG cubic beziers leaving the bottom of the caller and entering the
  top of the callee, with vertical control points so a curve meets a card
  square-on instead of grazing one it has nothing to do with.
- Pan is a pointer drag on the pane transform; zoom is anchored on the cursor,
  so the point under the pointer stays put instead of teleporting.
- ELK keeps doing layout, now asked for no edge routing: we draw our own curves,
  and reserving a lane per crossing edge was costing the map twice its width for
  routes that were then thrown away.

echarts is gone from this page entirely. The pure layer — breakCycles,
visibleGraph, scopeTo, filterSelection, folding — is renderer-agnostic and
survived untouched, as did its tests.

Also guards widgets.ts's shared resize batcher, which resolved every observed
element through `window.echarts` and threw once a page stopped loading it.

fix(service map): health on the right edge, service colour on the icon

The right-edge bar was carrying the service's hash colour, which is how Datadog
marks a node but not what Datadog puts *there* — theirs is a green/amber/red
health grade, and it reads without being looked at precisely because it means
one thing. Service identity moves to the icon, where it identifies without
competing.

Edges pick up the stronger stroke token and more resting opacity. At 0.12 on a
hairline they were technically present and practically invisible, which made the
map read as scattered cards rather than a flow.

Adds successColor and strokeStrong to getChartStyles; both tokens already exist
in the theme and neither was exposed.

feat(service map): orthogonal edges with rounded corners, as Datadog routes them

The beziers were wrong, not merely different. A curve between two distant cards
bows sideways through whatever sits between them, so in a dense row the eye
cannot tell which box an edge belongs to. Datadog's edges go down out of the
caller, across at a lane shared with their neighbours, then down into the
callee — and that shared lane is what makes them readable.

Corners are quarter-circles whose radius collapses as the run shortens, so a
short hop degrades to a straight line rather than overshooting its own corner,
and a vertically aligned pair is drawn as a plain line with no corners at all.

Tests pin the shape rather than the pixels: the horizontal run sits at the
midpoint, the turn goes the right way for a callee to the left, and the radius
never exceeds half the drop.

perf(service map): stop rebuilding the collapse map on every lookup

The page took 1.8s to render 31 services, most of it inside the graph fold
rather than the database — the read query answers in 28ms.

`domainOf` was bound as a function of the key:

    domainOf k = guard collapsing >> collapseMap [ ... ] k

so the association list and both Maps inside `collapseMap` were rebuilt on every
single lookup. It is called once per node from canon1, parentOf, rootOf and
climb, which makes the fold quadratic in node count with a Map construction as
the inner term. Bound as a value instead, the maps are built once.

Demo project, 31 nodes: 1.8s -> 0.25s. It scales with the square, so a real
project feels it far more: the one that prompted this has 221 distinct nodes,
roughly fifty times the wasted work.

The guard is a test with a stopwatch, because this bug produced no wrong output,
only a cost — nothing else in the suite would have caught it. 400 nodes folds in
milliseconds when the map is built once and takes long enough to be unmissable
when it is not.

refactor(service map): distillation pass

Combinators and Relude, where the hand-written form said nothing extra:

- `kindAt` was a case with an `(x : xs)` split and a foldl'. NKUnknown is the
  maximum NodeKind and a synthetic head's kindOf is exactly that, so the seed can
  never beat a real child: `foldr (min . kindAt) (kindOf k)` is total and one line.
- `memberCount` case on `[]`/`ks` -> `viaNonEmpty length`, the idiom already used
  in Utils and BackgroundJobs.
- The label's `maybe (…) (const …) (T.stripPrefix "rest:" key)` discarded the Just
  payload, so it was a predicate wearing a Maybe -> `bool` on `isPrefixOf`.
- `keptTop` was an identity list comprehension over `take nodeCap topLevel`, which
  was also computed a second time for `keptRoots`.

Drops the legacy rollup write. Nothing else writes that table once this deploys,
and the read path already prefers the env-dimensioned one per bucket and falls
back to the original only for buckets rolled before it existed — so the second
write bought nothing but a rollback window, at ~35 lines and a write per rollup.

Inlines the legend's Tailwind classes. They were hoisted into `where` bindings
and concatenated at the call site, which is the pattern the project rules single
out: the scanner has to see each class set as a literal on the element wearing
it, and a reader should not jump to a `where` clause to learn what a swatch looks
like. Costs two lines and is the right trade.

The perf guard forces with `evaluate` rather than `seq`, which in IO reads as if
it might not run at all.

fix(service map): honour the contracts the types were claiming

Constraint-evasion review. Six findings, one of which did not survive being
checked.

ServiceNode's haddock claimed at most one of memberCount/groupKey is ever set,
"so a head that is also a member never exists". Two-level collapse makes exactly
that node — a domain head that itself falls into the long tail — and the
TypeScript was changed to rely on it while the Haskell type kept asserting the
opposite. The tempting fix was a four-constructor sum, but all four combinations
of the two Maybes are reachable, so such a sum is isomorphic to the pair and
buys no safety: the documentation was the defect, not the encoding. Corrected,
and pinned with the test whose absence let it survive.

The collapsed group's health disclosure came back. A head's stats are the sum of
its members, so one endpoint failing outright inside forty healthy ones is a ~2%
aggregate — invisible, and precisely what the map exists to catch. The canvas
renderer said "3 of 42 returning errors" in its tooltip; the DOM rewrite kept the
members map that fed it, never read it, and titled the card with just a label.

'' is a storage detail and now stops at the boundary. The rollup column is NOT
NULL because it is in the primary key, so absence is stored as the empty string;
above envFromColumn it is Nothing, and the `not (T.null ev)` check that had to
re-derive "empty means unlabelled" downstream is gone.

Which kind of node a key denotes is structure, so it is asked structurally: the
synthesised tail heads are a Set, not a "rest:" prefix test on the string.

Also: NodeKind gains Bounded/Enum and a doctest pinning NKUnknown as the maximum,
which kindAt's fold silently depends on; the Collapse sum says "no cap" itself so
the maxBound sentinel is gone; and the rollup job's comment names the table it
actually writes.

No warning suppressions were added anywhere in the diff.

docs(service map): put the NodeKind ordering doctest in a Haddock block

doctest-parallel only extracts examples from Haddock comments, so the bare
`-- >>>` above the declaration would have been silently skipped — the same
silence the doctest was written to break.
fix(dashboards): route SQL by declared source
fix(migrations): repair dashboard SQL source migration
style(service-map): strengthen service map boundaries
otelcol memory limiter

fix(otelcol): silence tier-1 OTTL warn spam, qualify paths

Customer log bodies are arbitrary, so parse failures are expected input,
not operator signal. Three fixes:

- error_mode ignore -> silent: `ignore` logs a warn per record; the block
  comment already claimed failures were silent.
- ParseJSON requires a closing brace, skipping bodies truncated upstream
  before scanning the whole multi-KB string.
- ParseKeyValue skips JSON-shaped bodies: `key="{...}"` matched the logfmt
  prefix and split into thousands of failing pairs.

Parsed output is unchanged — these bodies yielded no attributes before
either. Also context-qualify every OTTL path (`log.body`), which the
collector was rewriting at startup and logging.

fix(docker): locate the built binary with cabal list-bin

`find dist-newstyle -name monoscope-server | head -1` picks an arbitrary match,
and dist-newstyle is a persistent BuildKit cache mount — so the copied binary
can be one left by an earlier build, compiled against a different static/ tree.
That shipped a prod image whose pages referenced a Vite entry chunk
(index.DiekaXWC.js) absent from the image: a 404 that killed every web
component on the page.

fix(assets): hash static asset URLs by path, not ?v= query

Cache busting via `?v=<hash>` is poisonable during a rolling deploy. CDNs key
on the path, and the server ignores the query entirely — it just streams the
file off disk — so a request for the new build's URL answered by a replica
still holding the old file caches those bytes under the new URL for the whole
max-age (a year). That happened on 2026-08-08: main.js was pinned to its
pre-htmx-4 version, whose top-level htmx.defineExtension('debug') throws under
htmx 4 and aborted the rest of the file, leaving window.updateGroupByButtonText
and everything after it undefined.

hashAssetFile now emits main.<hash>.js, and hashedAssetMiddleware maps the name
back to the file on disk. It verifies the hash rather than merely stripping it:
a replica that doesn't have the requested build must 404, or a stale one would
poison the new URL exactly as before.

The TS bundle references sprites and ECharts by path with no hash at all —
worse, since a newly added icon stays invisible to returning users for a year.
BodyWrapper now emits window.assetUrls with hashed URLs and web-components/src/
assets.ts reads it, which also folds together the two copies of faSprite_ and
drops a stale hardcoded ?v=ecf9d105.

fix(docker): copy shared/ and cli/ cabal files into the deps image

cabal.project lists shared/ and cli/ as packages, but Dockerfile.deps only
copied the root *.cabal — so `cabal configure` failed with "The package
location 'shared/' does not exist" on every deps-image build since the CLI
package split. Nothing gated on that failure, so the last-good deps image kept
serving deploys with a stale node_modules; once service-map.ts added elkjs, the
Vite build in the main image could no longer resolve it and every deploy
failed. Prod has been pinned to an old image for 26 commits as a result.

Only the .cabal files are copied, so editing sources doesn't invalidate the
dependency layer.

perf(log-patterns): index the unclassified-recent lookup

getLogPatternTextsByService was the most expensive statement in prod:
334k calls, 507ms mean, 47 hours cumulative, 145 TB of shared_blks_hit.
Its only usable index was (project_id, service_name) — no source_field and
nothing for the ORDER BY — so Postgres index-scanned every row for the
project/service (largest group: 1.83M), heap-fetched each to test
source_field and canonical_id, sorted by last_seen_at, then took 5000.
canonical_id IS NULL filters nothing today (3,980,129 of 3,980,129 rows),
so it removed no work while still forcing the heap visit.

Measured on the worst group before/after:

  without: 6419 ms, 1,662,683 buffers (13.3 GB), 4 parallel workers,
           top-N heapsort
  with   :   73 ms,     4,962 buffers (39 MB), plain index scan

88x faster, 335x fewer buffers. Index is 44 MB.

Created CONCURRENTLY in prod; this migration makes dev/staging match
(cf. 0083). IF NOT EXISTS, so it is a no-op on prod.

fix(web-components): resync package-lock so npm ci works again

package-lock.json pinned @emnapi/wasi-threads 1.2.2 while package.json's
tree resolved 1.2.3, so `npm ci` refused with EUSAGE. That broke three
things at once, all from the one cause:

  - the "Build Frontend" job (runs npm ci directly)
  - Dockerfile.deps (npm ci at line 60), so monoscope-deps:latest was
    never rebuilt after elkjs was added to package.json
  - the deploy build, which FROMs monoscope-deps:latest and therefore had
    no elkjs in node_modules:
      Rolldown failed to resolve import "elkjs/lib/elk.bundled.js"
      from web-components/src/service-map.ts

elkjs was declared correctly all along (dependencies, ^0.12.0, present in
the lock tree) — it just never got installed into the deps image.

Lock-only regeneration (npm install --package-lock-only): one optional
transitive dep, no node_modules or direct dependency changes.

fix(web-components): add linux-only optional deps to package-lock

Follow-up to 7a3f2b566, which only half-fixed this. That regeneration ran
on darwin/arm64, so npm resolved only the optional native bindings for
THIS platform and never wrote the linux/x64 ones into the lock. `npm ci`
consequently still failed on CI:

  Missing: @emnapi/core@1.11.3 from lock file
  Missing: @emnapi/runtime@1.11.3 from lock file

`npm ci --dry-run` passing locally was not evidence — it validates against
the current platform's optional deps only. Regenerated inside
node:22 on linux/amd64 (matching the CI runner) so both platforms'
optional bindings are recorded, and verified npm ci exits 0 under
linux/amd64 AND darwin/arm64.

Lock-only change; no direct dependency or node_modules changes.

fix(service map): unbreak the prod render, split the two explorer entries by kind

Three defects, one of which took the whole map down in production.

The filter input's `send "service-map-filter"(q: my value)` never parsed:
hyperscript reads an event name as an identifier path, so a dashed name ends
the token and the parser reports `Unexpected Token :` on the argument list —
costing the entire `_` attribute. It now `call`s a renderer-owned interop
function and the dashed wire event name stays where the TS contract wants it.

`buildCards`/`styleNode` reached every template hook through
`querySelector(...)!`, which erases at runtime. One hook missing — a drifted
template, or a cached bundle served against a newer one — threw mid-build and
left the map blank, which is the reported symptom. A missing hook now costs
that one detail.

`viz_type=traces` is not a viz type (`logs | timeseries | timeseries_line |
patterns | sessions`), so "View in trace search" fell through to the default
and landed on the plain log list, indistinguishable from "View logs". Spans
and logs genuinely are one surface here, so the two entries now differ by
kind — `kind!="log"` and `kind=="log"` — and both ask for a viz type that
exists.

The href construction moved to an exported `menuHref` so the kind split is
testable without a rendered map.

fix(log detail): show the whole identity, not whichever field won an alternative

The detail panel surfaced one identifier. `user.id` was emitted only when
`user.email` was absent, and then labelled "user name"; `user.full_name` and
`user.name` shared a slot so whichever lost was invisible; `user.hash` and
`session.previous.id` are promoted columns that were never rendered at all;
and tenant had no representation anywhere. Everything else was reachable only
by opening the Attributes JSON tree, which is why readers concluded we only
knew their email.

`identityFields` is now the single list of session/user/tenant keys — OTel
standardises `session.*`, `user.*` and `enduser.*` but has no tenant
convention, so the tenant keys are ones we choose to recognise, and that is a
decision that belongs in one place. The detail panel renders every field the
span carries from it, each as a filter pill, so "everything from this tenant"
is one click from the panel. The User & Session facets derive from the same
list instead of a hand-written five-entry copy that had already drifted;
they stay restricted to promoted columns, since a facet counts distinct values
and that needs a column rather than a probe into the Variant blob.

The log row still cannot afford eight badges, so it keeps one identity pill —
but the server now emits email, name and id under truthful labels and the
renderer folds them, so the tooltip names every identifier it has. The
abbreviated row identity is dropped from the detail header, where showing one
identifier beside all of them read as a contradiction.

Also repairs the NodeKind doctest, which asserted its invariant with
`maximum` — not exported by Relude — and so had been failing the whole
doctest suite.

feat(log list): make the latency column answerable — row-relative, by service or kind

Three things were wrong with it.

The colour was keyed on `span_name`, on both the server (`getServiceColors` over
the `span_name` column) and the client. "serviceColors" was therefore a
per-operation palette: two spans in one service got two colours, the same
operation in two services got one, and any name missing the palette fell back
to grey. It is now keyed on `service`, which is projected on every row and is
the same hash the trace waterfall and the service map use, so a service looks
the same wherever it appears.

The bar sat on the trace-wide axis, so a 3ms child inside a 2s trace was a
sub-pixel sliver — which is why child rows were unreadable — and the "frame"
drawn around such a row marked the bar's own bounds, three decorative lines
restating the bar. The row is now the axis: every row's bar is its own
duration, its direct children lay out inside it at their real offsets, and the
gaps between them are its self time. One rule at every depth. Trace position
moves into the title and aria-label, where it costs no pixels and, unlike a
colour, a screen reader can read it.

And the breakdown was hardcoded to one dimension. The latency column's existing
header dropdown now switches between `service` ("which service ate the
request") and `kind` ("was this my code or something it called"). Both columns
are already projected, so neither costs a query. Kind colours are fixed rather
than hashed, because they mean something; service colours stay hashed, because
they only identify.

`latencySegments` intersects each child against the row window rather than
clamping an offset: a child whose clock skewed it entirely before its parent
contributes nothing, instead of being pinned to the start of the bar as though
it happened there.

feat(environments): promote deployment.environment.name to a column and scope the app by it

Environment was reachable only as a probe into the `resource` blob, which is
why the service map had to grow its own env-dimensioned rollup table instead of
grouping by a column, and why an earlier env facet had to be reverted for
"querying a column Postgres does not have" (20506f4). otel_metrics has carried
`resource___deployment___environment___name` since 0108; spans and logs now do
too, on both stores.

The column is additive and nullable, so migration 0122 is O(1) on the
hypertable and TimeFusion evolves into it via SchemaMode::Merge. It is
deliberately not a TF sorting column — that list is load-bearing for the TopK
pushdown, and a low-cardinality column prunes badly by sort order and well by
row-group statistics, which it gets for free. No backfill: old rows keep their
environment in the Variant and read as unset, which the selector treats as
unknown rather than excluded.

The selection is a cookie read at auth time next to `theme` and `lang`, so it
rides on the session and every handler that already resolves one has it. A
query parameter was the original plan and was dropped: to be sticky it would
have to be declared on every route and threaded onto every link, since the
choice has to survive navigation to pages that never heard of it.

It is applied as `SqlQueryCfg.environment` → `nqEnvironment`, joining
`project_id` and the date range in the generated WHERE rather than being
spliced into the user's KQL — the query box must keep showing what the user
typed. That one seam covers every shape the builder emits, including the
monitor alert query, so a monitor scoped to staging cannot silently alert on
prod.

The picker offers the environments the project has actually reported, read from
the learned facet values, and hides itself entirely when there are none — a
picker whose only option is "All" is furniture.

Also seeds the two identity columns (`session.previous.id`, `user.hash`) into
the flattened-attribute fallback, which had drifted from the promoted set.

feat(errors): show the failing line's source, the way Sentry and Datadog do

A stack trace reached the error panel as one string and was rendered in a
`<pre>`. That told a reader nothing the string didn't already say, and it left
nothing for the panel to hang a source snippet on.

`Pkg.StackTrace` parses the string into frames — JS/Node, Python, Java/Kotlin,
Ruby, Go and PHP, chosen by the line's shape rather than by a declared
language, since the language is not on the span and a polyglot trace is a real
thing. The parse is total and loses nothing: a line matching no known shape
survives carrying its text, so recognising a frame is an upgrade and never a
filter.

Each frame renders as a native `<details>`, with the first in-app frame open —
Sentry's default, and the right one during an incident, since the top of a
stack is usually five frames of framework before anything you wrote. Opening a
frame fetches the source around its line from the repository already linked for
dashboard sync, and marks the failing line with a background AND a gutter
caret, never colour alone.

Source is read from the repo rather than uploaded: an uploaded snapshot is
source from whenever it was uploaded, while the repo can be read at a revision,
and the GitHub App installation is already there. A code mapping says how a
build path (`/srv/app/services/checkout.py`) lines up with a repo path
(`src/services/checkout.py`) — nothing can bridge those without being told.
Several per project, longest-prefix-first, because a project with two services
in two repos is the normal case. A frame no mapping claims resolves to nothing:
a wrong file rendered as the failing code is worse than no file.

The handler lives in its own module because the model reaches GitHub through
GitSync → Dashboards → Widget → LogItem, and putting it beside the renderer was
a cycle. `gitSyncToken` moved out of BackgroundJobs into GitSync so both callers
share one App-before-PAT precedence instead of two.

The issue view still renders its own <pre>: RuntimeException issues carry a
synthesised stack, a different shape from a span's exception.stacktrace, and
pointing this at it without checking those strings would be guessing.

feat(errors): use the OTel code.* frame when a runtime prints no stack

`frameFromAttributes` was written and then never called — dead on arrival.
Wiring it is the point: a runtime that follows OpenTelemetry's `code.*`
conventions has already told us the failing file, line and function, so a span
carrying those and no printed stack now gets a frame, and a source snippet,
instead of nothing at all. Sentry takes the same shortcut with SDK-attached
source context — the most reliable answer is the one the process itself
reported.

`framesFor` is the single decision about what there is to render, so the
disclosure and the renderer cannot disagree; two separate checks are how you
end up with a "Stack trace (0 frames)" control that opens onto nothing.

It takes a lookup rather than a map so it stays independent of how the caller
stores attributes — a span's are nested JSON values, not text.

fix(code context): give CodeMapping a Default, clearing two doctest-only imports

Data.UUID and fromGregorian were imported for the doctest alone, which GHC does
not see — so they read as unused and would fail a -Werror build. The catch-all
mapping (every frame, repo root, any service) is a real value worth naming, and

fix(sessions): fall back to user identity when session.id is absent

The Sessions viz keyed strictly on attributes___session___id, so every
project whose backend SDK cannot emit session.id showed an empty tab with
zeroed KPIs. Shipbubble is the live case: 0 session ids in 3 days of TF
data, because apitoolkit-express 3.x (sdk_type JsExpress) has no
setSession at all — only @monoscopetech/* does. They do emit user.id /
user.email on every request span.

Session identity is now one shared expression, sessionKeyExpr:
COALESCE(session.id, user.id, user.email). fetchSessions and the
ExpandSession filter in fetchEventExamples both use it, so a derived
session is listed *and* expandable. Projects that emit a real session.id
are unaffected; backend-only projects get one derived session per user
per selected window.

Verified against shipbubble's live TF data: 73 sessions / 63,499 events
in the last hour, ~2s.

fix(telemetry): render integral attribute numbers as plain digits

valText rendered every JSON number with show @Scientific, i.e.
formatScientific Generic: it appends ".0" and flips to exponent form above
7 digits. Every flattened attributes___* column goes through it, so a
numeric user.id of 806885555 was stored as "8.06885555e8".

That is not just a bad UI label. attributes.user.id is in
flattenedOtelAttributes, so KQL compiles it to the column — on prod today
`attributes.user.id == "806885555"` matches 0 rows while the mangled
"8.06885555e8" matches 4032. The Sessions viz inherits the same text as a
derived session key.

Integral values within Int64 now render as plain digits; non-integral and
out-of-range values keep the old rendering (guarding against a huge
exponent materialising an Integer). Doctested through atMapText, the
exported path the columns take.

No backfill: already-stored rows keep the old text, so a numeric-id user's
derived sessions can split across two keys inside a window spanning the
deploy. That self-heals as data ages out, and a TF-wide UPDATE is exactly
the hash-update storm that has OOM-crashed the service before.

feat(code context): source repos are their own thing, not the config-sync repo

0123 hung a code mapping off `projects.github_sync`, which is
UNIQUE (project_id) and holds the ONE repo monoscope syncs its own
dashboard/monitor YAML with. A project's services live in as many repos
as they like, and that is a different question from where its config
lives — so the design made every repo but the config one unreachable, and
`fetchSnippet` refused any mapping that did not point at it.

Migration 0124 splits them:

  * `github_sync`        — one repo per project, monoscope's own YAML. Untouched.
  * `github_credentials` — many per project, one per GitHub account, holding
    the App installation. An installation already reaches every repo in that
    account, which is why auth belongs here and not on a per-repo row.
  * `code_mappings`      — now names owner/repo/ref itself, authorised by a
    credential. Adding the tenth service repo costs a mapping, not an
    integration.

Existing 0123 mappings are carried across: a credential is minted from the
sync row's grant and the coordinates copied onto the mapping. One that
cannot be reconstructed is dropped — it could only ever have rendered
"no longer linked" anyway.

fix(kql): validate fields against the source the caller asked for

Field validation (da40e8ef) has had the unit suite red since 2026-08-08 —
48 ParserSpec examples plus the dashboard-template spec — and the failures
were not all stale expectations. Three real defects behind them:

  * `parseQueryToComponents` validated against `otel_logs_and_spans` even
    when the source came from the request rather than the query text, so a
    Metrics-page query naming `metric_name`/`value` was rejected as an
    unknown field. `parseQueryDiagnosed` now takes the caller's source, the
    same way `queryASTToComponents` already resolves the FROM table from it.
  * `method` named no column, so the shipped http-stats and kitchensink
    dashboards — and the apitoolkit-era saved queries that spell it that
    way — stopped rendering. It joins `span_name`/`service`/`trace_id` as an
    alias for `attributes___http___request___method`.
  * The builtin column list had drifted from the table in both directions.
    It carried `updated_at` and `deleted`, which are not columns here, so a
    query naming them passed validation and then died at the database —
    precisely the failure validation exists to prevent. And it was missing
    21 flattened attributes the table does have, `attributes.error.type`
    among them, which the app's own generated queries use: on the server the
    startup introspection papered over it, but `monoscope validate` and the
    tests have no database and turned those queries away.

The list stays hand-written; it is only the fallback for callers with no
database, since the server unions it with a live information_schema read.

The spec's remaining failures were expectations: it filtered on invented
fields (`method`, `Computer`, `status`, `user_id`, `error_message`, `count`)
whose expected SQL asserted a column no table has, so those queries could
only ever have failed at the database. They now name real columns. Six more
pinned megaparsec's caret diagram, which da40e8ef replaced with the one-line
rendering a toast can actually show.

Three widgets aggregated `value` against `otel_logs_and_spans`, which has no

feat(issues): acknowledging an issue silences it, and the silence has an end

"Acknowledged" promised nothing. It moved a row out of the Inbox and kept
sending alerts, so the only way to actually stop being paged was to archive —
which also meant "this isn't worth fixing". The word had no meaning you could
act on, and the Acknowledged tab was where issues went to be forgotten.

How the others resolve it: Sentry's Archive takes an explicit "until" (a
duration, or until it happens again N times) and stops notifying for it.
Datadog keeps monitor muting time-boxed and separate from status. PagerDuty's
ack is "I'm on it" with a timeout that re-pages if nothing happens.

The common thread is that silence is a promise with an expiry. So rather than
adding a second verb next to acknowledge, acknowledge *becomes* the silence
control — one concept, with a window:

  Open        needs triage                        notifies
  Acknowledged someone owns it, until <when>      silent, then back to Inbox
  Archived    not actionable                      silent, stays hidden

- apis.issues gains acknowledged_until (0125). A far-future sentinel — the same
  one monitors use for an indefinite mute — encodes "until it regresses".
  It supersedes cooldown_until, which said the same thing but only for
  log_pattern_rate_change and only for a fixed 24h.
- The notification paths honour it. claimIssueNotification, the new-endpoint
  claim, and the error-subscription sweep all now skip acknowledged and
  archived issues; a lapsed ack stops blocking immediately rather than waiting
  on the sweep. This is the actual bug: none of them looked at ack state before.
- Detectors consult isSilenced before firing a fresh issue for a target, so an
  ack means "don't tell me about this again", not "hide the old row".
- expireLapsedAcks (in the 10-min notification sweep) returns timed acks to the
  Inbox with an ack_expired activity event, so one can't rot out of sight.
- UI: the acknowledge control is a split button — one click silences until it
  regresses, the caret offers 1h/4h/8h/1d/3d/1w. Rows and the detail header
  show the time left; each tab says in one line what it means for notifications.
  Bulk actions now offer only the transitions that make sense from the tab
  you're on. Ack and archive were <a> without href: not keyboard-operable.
  They are buttons now, and the icon-only row actions have accessible names.
- API/CLI: POST /issues/:id/ack?duration_minutes=, issues bulk duration_minutes,
  monoscope issues ack --for MINUTES. Absent duration = indefinite, which is
  what ack did before, so existing callers keep their semantics.

The duration menu and its "4h left" label are shared with monitor muting, so
"for how long?" is answered the same way in both places.

fix(notifications): an explicit "Notify every N" subscription no longer expires

The 10-min sweep picked a project only if it had an error pattern created in
the last 24h. That bound sat on the row, so a subscription on an older pattern
was never swept — the project was never handed to sweepErrorSubscriptions at
all, and the cadence just stopped. It looked like it worked because the
post-ingestion inline path has no such bound, so re-notification kept happening
for exactly as long as the error kept re-occurring, and died the moment it went
quiet.

The 24h ceiling is a bound on *automatic* eligibility — it stops the sweep
alerting on ancient rows nobody asked about. An explicit subscription is the
opposite: someone asked. So it now sits outside the ceiling rather than under
it. The claim query downstream already had no age bound on the subscription
clause, so this is purely a project-selection fix.

Verified against the real schema before the test existed: with a 3-day-old
subscribed pattern seeded, the old predicate selects 0 projects and the new one
selects 1.

ci: gate the deploy on the test job, and give that job time to finish

`build-and-deploy` had `if: always()` and no `needs`, so the CapRover deploy
ran in parallel with the tests and shipped whatever the tests said. Combined
with a `timeout-minutes: 30` the job could not fit inside, master has been
deploying unverified: on 97f4ef84 the wall landed on the doctests (unit, cli
and integration never ran), and on fbf99a06 it landed on the integration suite.
Which step gets truncated is a function of cache luck, not of the change.

Split the old job in two. Pushing the image is harmless whatever the tests say
— nothing runs it until something deploys it — so `build-image` keeps no
`needs` and stays parallel with the tests, off the critical path. The new
`deploy` job carries `needs: [build-image, build-and-test]` and no `if`, so a
failed, cancelled or timed-out test job leaves it skipped and the image sits in
the registry unused. Time-to-prod grows by whatever the tests still have left
to run when the image is ready, not by the whole suite.

Raising the timeout to 60 is part of the gate, not separate from it: at 30 the
job self-truncates, and a truncated job would now block every deploy. Measured
floor with a warm cache is ~30m before the integration suite even starts (~1.5m
containers, 5.5m hpack, 16m build, 6m doctests), so 60 leaves room for a cold one.

Worth a follow-up: `Install hpack` compiles from source on every run and costs
5.5 minutes of that budget.

fix(cli): a bare search term is full-text again, not an unknown field

`monoscope logs search POISON_ROW_DROPPED` — the example in the command's own
--help and in docs/cli.md — has been exiting with

    invalid query: Unknown field "POISON_ROW_DROPPED"

since field validation landed in e7ad369. Nothing was wrong with the search
itself: `buildSearchParams` rewrites a bare term into `body has "X" or summary
has "X"` before it goes on the wire, and that is valid. But `validateEventsOpts`
validated `opts.query` — the raw term, before the rewrite — so the parser was
asked to resolve a search term as a column and the CLI exited before the rewrite
ever ran.

Validate the text that will actually be sent. Confirmed in ghci against this
tree: parseQueryToAST "chunkevt" is Left, and the rewritten form is Right.

Server-side is unaffected: the API only ever received the rewritten query, so
this was never visible through the web UI or a direct API call.

The two halves drifting apart is the actual defect, so the doctests on
rewriteBareQuery now assert that its output parses, not just what it looks like.

refactor(issues): read issues through selectFrom, not SELECT *

Four queries decoded `SELECT * FROM apis.issues` positionally into `Issue`, so
the record's field order had to track the table's attnum order, and adding a
column changed the shape of a row every already-running binary was still
decoding. Migration 0125 hit exactly that window: during a rolling deploy an old
container reads 31 columns into a 30-field record and 500s on issue reads until
it is replaced. 0075 and 0085 had the same exposure.

`selectFrom @Issue` emits the column list from the record's own fields, which
makes decoding independent of both physical order and later additions.
`selectIssueByIdScoped` and `selectIssuesByFilters` already did this; this just
finishes the job. The stale attnum comment on the record is replaced with the
reason, since that comment is what a future ADD COLUMN will read.

Also records why acknowledging silences an explicit "Notify every N"
subscription on the same issue — ack is the later and more specific
instruction, and a silence that leaks one channel is not a silence — and names
the one-line change that would invert it, at the line that would have to change.

feat(git): git integration stops meaning GitHub

GitLab (SaaS and self-hosted), Gitea/Forgejo and Bitbucket Cloud all expose
the six operations the code-context and config-sync features need — read a
tree, read a file, write a file, list repositories, report a default branch,
verify a webhook signature. `Pkg.Git` makes the host a value and the dialect a
case expression, where `api.github.com` used to be hardcoded at every call.

Schema follows in 0125: `github_sync`/`github_credentials` become
`git_sync`/`git_credentials` with `host` and `api_base` columns, and
`last_tree_sha` becomes `last_revision` — a resolved head commit, which every
host can report and which answers the only question that column was ever
asked. The auth checks become host-aware: only GitHub has an App
installation, so an `installation_id` on any other host is a row nothing could
act on. `(project_id, account)` becomes `(project_id, host, account)`, since
`acme` on GitHub and `acme` on GitLab are different grants.

0126 leaves auto-updatable views under the old table names. The runner
migrates on start-up, so the schema moves the moment any instance boots —
including one running the previous build, whose queries all name the old
tables. Without the views, GitHub sync breaks for the length of a rolling
deploy. Drop them once no instance runs older code.

The new hosts ship behind `ENABLE_NON_GITHUB_GIT_HOSTS`, off by default:
their URL building and JSON decoding are covered by doctests and fixtures but
have never run against those vendors' live APIs. GitHub is unaffected.

See plans/07-git-hosts.md.

fix(log explorer): colour a collapsed row's latency bar by the whole subtree

`childrenTimeSpans` carried only the direct children, so a collapsed trace row
was coloured by whatever its immediate child happened to be. The service that
actually spent the time is usually deeper — an API span whose only child is
another span of the same service read as one flat colour — so the bar answered
"where did this request go?" with the least useful level of the tree.

It now carries every descendant with a depth relative to the row, and
`exclusiveSegments` attributes each interval to the deepest span covering it.
Exclusive rather than cumulative: nested spans would otherwise bill the same
microseconds to every ancestor and make the segments sum past the row's own
duration. The waterfall still asks for depth 1 only, since it draws each
descendant as its own row.

feat(live-tail): stream matching logs from the ingest path over SSE

Adds Live Tail as the Explorer's first tab. Events stays the landing route — "what
happened" is the question people arrive with; watching a stream is one they choose.

The Events tab answers by querying TimeFusion. Live Tail can't: the row a user is
waiting for hasn't been written yet. So matching happens on the ingest pod, on the
in-memory record, before the durable write, and the matched row is pushed sideways
to whichever web pod holds that user's SSE connection.

Three pieces bridge ingest and web, which are separate processes:

  * A leased subscription row in Postgres (0125). Web pods write what the browser
    wants; ingest pods poll unexpired rows into a cache. It's a lease because every
    failure that matters — crashed tab, killed pod, sleeping laptop — loses the
    DELETE. The browser renews; nothing else does.
  * A Kafka side-topic carrying only rows that already matched, keyed by
    subscription id. A project nobody tails costs one HashMap lookup and produces
    nothing.
  * A per-pod hub. Every web pod consumes the whole topic under its own group,
    since any browser may land on any pod.

Filtering reuses Pkg.Parser.Expr through a second interpreter (Pkg.Parser.Eval)
rather than a new filter language, so a query means the same thing in both tabs by
construction. Its contract is parity with the SQL the AST already lowers to, not
with Haskell intuition or upstream KQL — missing fields are NULL and fail every
comparison including negated ones, JSON null is NULL too, and `has` matches
substrings because that is what the SQL side emits. Undecidable filters count as
non-matches: failing open would leak rows nobody asked for.

Live Tail sits inside the ingestion path, which is not a convenience feature. Every
failure here — stale cache, broken filter, dead broker, slow browser — degrades the
tail and leaves the telemetry write untouched.

The transport keys off whether Kafka brokers are configured, deliberately not
enableKafkaService: that flag is per-process, so web pods (off) and ingest pods (on)
would pick different transports — web serving a hub nobody publishes to while ingest
publishes to a topic nobody consumes. Broker config is what both roles share.

Enabled by default; a broker-configured deployment with no topic refuses outright
rather than accepting subscriptions it could never feed.

The integration suite had not run in CI for some time (the job kept hitting its

parses an event name as an identifier path — the dashed name was a parse error

guarding the bug. It now asserts the `call` and fails if the dashed form returns.

Pages.QueryCache used `totally_made_up_column` to provoke a *backend* failure.

before any SQL is built, so `seedCache` dies in `parseQueryToAST` with a

parser's message reaches the widget. The three guards that need a genuine

build: make running TimeFusion locally actually work, and document it

Specs behind `withTfReads True` and the dual-write TF leg only test anything
when TimeFusion is reachable. Without it they fail locally and pass in CI, and
a real regression is easy to file as "just the missing service" — which is
exactly the mistake that let two genuine LogExplorer failures sit unexamined.

`make timefusion-start` existed and already ran TF natively, but never worked:
the recipe was `export … && port=… && nohup cargo run … & echo … && for …`, and
`A && B && C & D` backgrounds `A && B && C`, so `port` was assigned inside the
background job while the readiness loop polled `nc -z 127.0.0.1 ` with it empty.
It burned the full 900s timeout every time and never reported ready. Fixed in
the timefusion checkout by sourcing the env into the current shell and
backgrounding only cargo; `tf-stop` now kills the process group, since `cargo
run` spawns the server as a child and killing the recorded pid orphaned
something still holding :12345.

New here:
- live-test-dev-tf: the sanctioned watcher with TF wired in. Previously the only
  TF path was test-integration-tf, which shells out to `cabal test` against this
  repo's own rule, so the inner loop had no TF option at all.
- tmux-timefusion: `timefusion-start` backgrounds with nohup, which an agent
  harness or CI wrapper reaps — TF bound :12345 and died seconds later. A pane
  outlives its creator.
- timefusion-status: cheaper than misreading a test failure.

Also: CI sets TIMEFUSION_BUFFER_FLUSH_IMMEDIATELY, which TimeFusion does not
read — its envy-derived BufferConfig exposes TIMEFUSION_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECS
(default 60) and TIMEFUSION_FLUSH_DWELL_SECS. I copied that setting here before
checking, so the docs now name the real knobs and warn against the dead one.

The editor underlines whatever `/log_explorer/validate` returns, and that

feat(live-tail): Events streams the same push path, with no Kafka requirement

Three changes on top of the initial Live Tail commit: the Events tab's live toggle
now uses the push path, Live Tail needs no configuration, and it no longer needs
Kafka.

Events' live mode was a 5s poll re-running the cursor query. That could never be
made fast: a row waits for its ingest batch and then has to land in TimeFusion
before any query returns it, so the interval was bounded below by write-visibility
latency no matter how short it got. An SSE "something changed" nudge would have
been worse — it fires from the pre-write hook, so it necessarily precedes the data
it announces, and turns one push into a full query. The only way under that floor
is to read the record before it is written, which is what the push path does.

`Scope = LogsOnly Text | AllSignals` replaces the bare service field, so the
service gate is structural: Live Tail cannot be constructed without a service and
Events has nowhere to put one. That was previously a NOT NULL plus a handler check
— a pair the second surface would have had to lie to. `LiveRow` became a sum for
the same reason, and the Scope that picks the subscription picks the shape.

Column projection can't be derived server-side (a query's final columns may be SQL
expressions only the database can evaluate), so the browser sends its own list and
ingest resolves each name by mapping ___ back to a path, reusing the filter
evaluator's resolver. One traversal rule serves matching and rendering, so a field
that filters correctly also renders correctly.

Kafka is the queue this system is built around but it is optional infrastructure:
dev, docker-compose and self-hosted installs run without it, and a feature that
quietly does nothing there does not work. Postgres is not optional, so it is the
floor — an UNLOGGED relay table (0127) carries matched rows when no brokers are
configured. No new dependency. The in-process hub is gone because choosing it
required knowing whether ingest and HTTP share a process, which no process can
tell; guessing was silently wrong for every split deployment without Kafka.

All eight LIVE_TAIL_* environment variables are deleted. None was a deployment
decision — they are the shape of the feature, and an operator asked to pick a lease
length has no way to answer. The one thing that varies, whether Kafka exists, is
read from kafkaBrokers.

Fixes found while building this, each with a regression guard:

  * Pushed rows never rendered. groupSpans keys its tree off trace adjacency, not
    the row array, and pushed rows were passed an empty traces list — so it
    returned an empty tree every time. The feature would have looked inert with
    nothing in the logs to explain it.
  * Live Tail could not start at all: the service dropdown read a response key the
    schema endpoint has never returned, and the service gate is hard. The
    environment selector was never populated either.
  * Subscription limits were counted, checked, then inserted across three round
    trips. Now one conditional INSERT. Still approximate under READ COMMITTED, and
    said so where it matters.
  * The relay decoded rows without the envelope version check the Kafka path uses,
    so a rolling-deploy skew was indistinguishable from corruption; and its buffer
    dropped rows on overflow without counting them.
  * handleLiveRows dropped rows whenever logsContainer was null. The container
    decides where a row goes, never whether it arrives.

Navigating away deletes the subscription, and the SSE handler deletes it on
teardown too — the server learns a connection died the moment the body fails,
which beats waiting out the lease for a crashed tab. Matching stops within one
cache refresh rather than one lease.

perf(issues): stop the Logs tab dumping the whole retention window

An issue with no trace id rendered the Logs tab as `context___trace_id==""`,
a predicate that filters nothing: the tab returned the same rows, in the same

Log records carry no trace context (99.4% of them, measured on prod TF) while
spans always do, so 5313/22335 error patterns (24%) have no trace id and hit
this path. With no trace to pin to, scope to the issue's service over a +/-5min
window around when it was last seen.

log-list also fetched on connectedCallback even though the tab is display:none
until opened, so that query ran for a panel the user never looked at. Embedded
lists (initialFetchUrl set) now defer to first visibility; the log explorer
itself stays eager.

Page load 6.5s -> ~400ms; the tab costs 1.2s when actually opened.

fix(db): project entity columns explicitly instead of SELECT *

`SELECT *` decoded positionally into a Generic DecodeRow breaks the moment a
migration adds a column: the decoder expects N and gets N+1, and every read of
that table 500s until the binary is redeployed. This happened live today —
`acknowledged_until` landed on apis.issues and every issue read failed with
`UnexpectedColumnCountStatementError 30 31`.

fix(live tail): match on the direct OTLP path, not only the queue path

The ingest hook lived only in dualWriteWithPoisonMapping, which is the path
telemetry takes through Kafka or Pub/Sub. Records arriving over OTLP directly
-- gRPC on 4317, and OTLP/HTTP -- go through processSignalRequest and write
straight to the store, with no hook. In any deployment without a queue in
front (every dev box, docker-compose and self-hosted install, and any prod pod
taking OTLP directly) a tail registered fine, reported live, held its SSE
connection open, and matched nothing, ever.

The fibers stop guessing the topology too. live-tail-cache was gated on
enableKafkaService || enablePubsubService || enableOtlpGrpcService, which is
an inference about "does this process ingest?" that OTLP/HTTP falsifies -- it
arrives on the ordinary web listener with none of those set. A pod that
ingests without a refreshed cache matches every record against an empty
subscription list. Same lesson as removing LocalHub: the cost was never the
fiber, it was the guess. The cache and both relay fibers now always run; an
idle refresh is one indexed query every 2s and the relay reader skips its
query entirely while this pod holds no connections.

Also closes the four gaps found reviewing the plan against the code:

- SSE responses now set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform and
  X-Accel-Buffering: no, and text/event-stream is excluded from the gzip
  middleware. Compression is the one buffering hop a response header cannot
  opt out of, and the size threshold alone would hold the first 860 bytes.
- The server can speak: a Notice row crosses the same addressed path as a row
  and surfaces as an SSE frame. Sent when a stored filter stops compiling --
  previously that tail died silently and went on reporting live. Named
  `notice`, not `error` as the plan had it: EventSource dispatches on the
  frame name, so `error` lands on onerror and gets retried, making the one
  event meaning "retrying will not help" the one guaranteed to retry.
- Envelopes are capped whole, not just per field. 128 columns at the 8000-char
  field cap is past Kafka's 1 MiB default, so the shape was reachable; over
  the cap the row is dropped and counted rather than handed to a broker that
  will refuse it.
- A per-batch evaluation budget bounds subscriptions x batch size, the product
  nothing bounded before. Records beyond it are counted as skipped, never
  silently unevaluated.

Fixes a second live defect found by the new tests: countActiveForUser and
countActiveForProject selected count(*)::int (int4) while the Int decoder
expects int8, so both threw. They run only when an insert has been refused, to
name which cap was hit -- so "you have too many live tails open" reached the

perf(code-context): cache source blobs, so a stack trace is one fetch not one per frame

`fetchSnippet` called the git host once per frame opened, and a hot issue viewed
repeatedly re-fetched every time. A rate-limited fetch presents as the panel
silently not filling in, which reads as "this feature is broken" rather than as
a quota — so this was the gate on turning source context on by default for large
projects.

Keyed `(owner, repo, ref, path)` in an `AuthContext` cache, the same shape as
`hostStatsCache`/`endpointStatsCache`. NOT `Pkg.QueryCache`, which the plan
suggested — that module is a timeseries cache (bins, windows, merge-on-overlap)
and fits a blob fetch badly.

Scope of the caching is deliberately narrow:

- Only the blob fetch. The mapping lookup, credential decrypt and token exchange
  still run every time, so a revoked credential fails on the next view rather
  than 15 minutes later.
- Only successes. Caching a failure would pin a transient 502 on screen for the
  whole TTL.
- Not project-scoped: the same public repo linked by two projects is the same
  bytes, and the credential that fetched it is not part of the file's identity.
  Access is still checked per request before any lookup happens.

15-minute TTL because the key cannot tell a mutable ref (a branch) from an
immutable one (a sha), so the shorter bound wins.

The test counts outbound requests through a fake HTTP interpreter and asserts a
second frame in the same file costs nothing — a PAT credential means no token
exchange, so every request it sees is the blob fetch with nothing to subtract.

  queue is full -- those spans are written and queryable but never enriched,
  so nothing downstream looks wrong and the counter is the only place it
  shows.
- drain flushes completed, spans flushed, patterns persisted.
- dashboard widget SQL errors.

Two details worth keeping in mind when adding more:

- Instruments must be created once, so each is a top-level NOINLINE binding
  over mkCounter/mkHist rather than built at a call site.
- Metrics.count treats zero as a no-op. Most call sites fold a batch and add
  whatever came out, and most batches produce nothing -- recording those
  would mint a series for every attribute combination that never happened.
- Browser drop counts are cumulative per connection (the UI renders a total),
  so the SSE handler holds the last reported value and adds only the delta.
  Feeding the running total to a counter would re-count every drop on every

fix(metrics): give the Live Tail fiber counters a span, so they carry exemplars

Exemplars are automatic under the SDK's default TraceBased filter -- a
measurement recorded while a sampled span is in context gets a trace/span id
attached, and a spike on a chart becomes clickable. The inverse is the trap:
recorded outside a span you get nothing, silently, because the counter still
moves and nothing fails.

runBackground interprets the Tracing effect but never opens a span, so every
fiber-side Live Tail counter was landing bare. The ingest-path counters were
always fine -- dualWriteWithPoisonMapping and processSignalRequest are both
inside spans -- which is exactly why the gap was invisible.

Spans are opened only on ticks that record something, never per tick. The
relay poller runs four times a second and the cache refresher every two; a
span each would be hundreds of thousands of spans per pod per day describing
nothing happening. Overflow, rejected filters and decode failures are rare, so
the baseline stays zero and the exemplar exists exactly when someone wants to
drill into it.

liveTailCacheLoaded stays outside a span on purpose. It is a level, not an
event -- nobody drills from "500 subscriptions loaded" into a trace.

reportSkew and liveTailConsumer take a TracerProvider now, since both need one
to open the span.

off the scroll signal the virtualiser already emits — no new listener to leak.

`atInsertionEdge` replaces both the old inline test and the private `atNewRowEdge`

whether to buffer, whether to flush, whether to anchor while inserting — and two
spellings disagreed between 0 and 2 pixels: the batch inserted because it was at the
edge, then anchored because it wasn't, scrolling the old top row back over the rows
just streamed in. Covered for both insertion paths, the recent fetch and the SSE push.

fix(log-list): stop clipping row tooltips to the height of their row

Rows carried `contain: layout style paint`, and paint containment clips every
descendant to the row's own box — 28px. Measured, the device badge's tooltip carries
a full user-agent string, renders 61px tall, and was left less than half visible.
Every other in-row tooltip (timestamp, replay, summary badges and icons) is clipped

the one declarative route into the top layer, `interestfor`, only invokes from a link
or a button — so keeping it would mean turning `<span>` labels into controls.

Dropping `paint` gives up little. The virtualiser already removes off-screen rows from
the DOM, so it was not saving their paint; layout and style containment are what keep
one row's contents from affecting its siblings, and both stay. A test pins the absence
so it cannot quietly return. If row scrolling regresses, that one line is the revert.

fix(log-list): resume live tail on scroll too, and cover the flipped direction

Resuming was driven only by the virtualiser's visibility event, which does not fire
when the first row is already on screen and the last few pixels of scroll close the
gap — the exact position the buffer strands at. A scroll binding on the container
closes it; declared in the template, so lit removes it with the element and there is
no teardown to leak. The visibility hook stays: it covers a jump straight to the top
that never crosses the intermediate positions.

Oldest-first had no component-level coverage. The predicate was tested, but anything
reading a real container passes regardless under jsdom, where every height is 0 and so
every container reports itself pinned to the bottom. Stubbing the container makes the
direction expressible: at the top, flipped, the buffer must hold — that is the far end
of the list, not the edge new rows arrive at.

test(live-stream): cover lease renewal, backoff and release

The lifecycle tests covered registration, drops, refusal, the notice-vs-retry split
and expiry. Three things the client owns were untested, and each fails silently:

- Renewal timing. The browser holds the lease alive, so a renewal that never fires is
  a tail that dies at the lease length with no error. Pinned to a third of the server's
  own expiry — a client renewing on a stale local constant lets the lease lapse under it
  — and to the 5s floor that stops an expired-by-skew lease becoming a renewal storm.
- Reconnect backoff. A fixed retry against a broken backend is a self-inflicted load
  test; the ladder is the thing that makes a long outage cost fewer attempts.
- Release on stop. A lease left behind keeps matching on the ingest pods until it expires.

Also records the decision that a bar and its card list different sets on an expanded
row: the bar has become a waterfall, the card stays a breakdown of the subtree.

feat(log-explorer): a legend naming where the whole result set spent its time

The card answers "what is this row waiting on". Nothing answered "what dominates
these results", and until something names them the colours in the bars are
write-only — a colour you have to hover a row to decode is one you decode once per
row. The mapping is stable (a service is coloured by a hash of its name, the same in
the service map and the waterfall), so reading it once here teaches it everywhere.

Each row contributes its self time — its duration minus what its direct children were
doing — to its own service. Billing whole durations would charge a request's time to
every service in its call chain and total past the wall clock; self time partitions
one real quantity, so the shares mean something. Concurrent children are merged rather
than added, since two siblings running at once occupy one stretch of their parent.

Ordered by that time, capped at six with the remainder counted, and hidden entirely
when there is nothing to disambiguate: one service is its own legend, and spending a
row of a dense table to say "api 100%" is worse than saying nothing.

the FILTER form the sessions query uses.

per session, where the sketch is exact anyway (exact below 512 distinct).

perf(metrics): one INSERT shape for otel_metrics, not ~350

`insertOtelMetrics` built its SQL as `chunksOf 350` rows with one `(…)` tuple
per row IN THE STATEMENT TEXT. Full chunks are all 350, but every call's ragged
tail is a different size, so over time the workload mints ~350 distinct
statement texts — each a distinct prepared statement and a distinct cached plan,
and each carrying 350 x 68 ~= 23,800 bind params that TimeFusion's insert
coercion wraps individually in a CAST. Prod 2026-08-14: TF's plan cache sat at
