fix(log-explorer): stop the freeze, the stuck loader and the blank list

Three independent defects behind the "browser locks up / had to reload"
reports, all reproduced against a real project before fixing.

Detail panel stranded on a loading spinner. htmx 4 defaults to
`hx-sync: queue first`, so clicking a second row while a detail request was
in flight *dropped* the new request: the row never loaded, and since the
indicator is flagged on click but only cleared by a request that actually
runs, the spinner stayed until a page reload. #log_details_container now
carries hx-sync="this:replace" so the newest click aborts the in-flight one,
and the client always hands the loader back on settle, keyed by a request
sequence so a superseded request cannot clear the winner's indicator. The
indicator is re-queried rather than cached, since it lives inside the
container the response innerHTML-swaps.

List going permanently blank. Once the retention window evicts,
lit-virtualizer can settle into rendering no rows while items is non-empty,
and never recovers on its own: nothing renders, so nothing changes, so no
update or scroll event ever arrives to notice. Recovered by a watchdog that
resets the scroll origin to force a re-measure and returns the user to the
row they were reading, budgeted per eviction.

Unbounded trace tree in the worker. flattenSpanTree gave every node a full
copy of its descendant subtree - a 2000-span deep trace produced ~2,000,000
segment objects, all structured-cloned worker to main - and neither it nor
bubbleIdentity guarded against a cycle, so a malformed parent chain was a
RangeError. Subtree segments are now capped (trimmed by duration; real
traces are ~3 deep and never reach it), with a visited set and a depth
bound. buildTraceTree had the same gap server-side, where it is an infinite
loop holding a database connection; it now carries a visited set and prunes
back-edges so the adjacency sent to clients is acyclic.

Also cuts main-thread work: MAX_RETAINED_ROWS 5000 -> 2500, memoised
cssTokenToHex (getComputedStyle forced a style recalc on every scroll tick),
and scrollToIndex instead of element().scrollIntoView when restoring the
scroll anchor - also a correctness fix, since element() only resolves
already-rendered rows, so off-screen anchors were never pinned.

Measured at 4x CPU throttle: click+scroll stress 6.0-8.8s -> 2.8-4.6s of
main-thread blocking per round, worst task ~800ms -> ~400ms.

Carries the in-progress query-library extraction, which shares Log.hs and
cannot compile apart from it.

fix(metrics): report SUBMITTED rows, not rowsAffected, under ON CONFLICT

d9e58f662 moved otel_metrics onto the shared `unnestInsert` machinery. That
machinery returns `rowsAffected`, and the metrics PG leg carries
`ON CONFLICT (project_id, timestamp, id) DO NOTHING` — so a replayed export
legitimately affects ZERO rows while losing nothing, because the conflicting row
is already durable.

`unaccountedRows` cannot tell a skipped duplicate from a dropped row. Feeding it
`rowsAffected` therefore made every replay look like silent under-persistence:
it raises `SilentUnderPersistError`, which becomes `Left WriteFailure`, which the
gRPC handler reports as "OTLP write failed: pg-failed" and sends the batch to the
DLQ.

The VALUES implementation this replaced used `interpExecute_` and hard-coded
`V.length records` for exactly this reason, carrying the comment "a chunk either
lands whole or throws". Moving to a statement that returns `rowsAffected`
silently changed that contract.

This is what has kept master undeployable since 2026-08-14 16:11Z, red on two
pre-existing specs in `Opentelemetry.GrpcIngestion`:

  - "deduplicates replayed metric exports by deterministic raw-point id" —
    ingests the same point twice and expects one row, so the second export
    affects zero.
  - "Test 7.1: should complete end-to-end integration" — ingests the same
    metric name/value/timestamp for three keys of ONE project, so points two
    and three collide on the deterministic id.

Both are explained by this and by nothing else; the earlier suspicion of the
`numArrayColumn` / `string_to_array(_, chr(31))::T[]` SQL was wrong. Diffing the
distinct `UTC [pid] ERROR:` lines of the green baseline run against the red one
shows an IDENTICAL set — `pg-failed` never corresponded to a Postgres server
error at all, which is what pointed at row accounting instead of SQL.

`bulkInsertOtelLogsAndSpans` is deliberately left alone: it has no `ON CONFLICT`,
so affected and submitted are the same number there. That asymmetry is why spans
survived the same refactor and metrics did not.

ci: let anyone run CI, and let CI skip what was already proven (#491)

CI re-runs work that has already been done: a PR run proves a tree, the squash
merge keeps that exact tree, and master builds and tests all of it again. On
4-vCPU runners that is ~20 minutes per push, and none of that capacity is
available to a developer whose laptop is faster than the runner.

ci/checks.tsv is now the one definition of what CI is; the workflows and
scripts/ci/ci.sh both read it. Each check is fingerprinted over the git blob
hashes of its declared inputs, and a pass publishes an attestation as a ref:

  refs/ci-attest/v1/<check>/<fingerprint>/<platform>/<capabilities>/<date>

A gate job resolves those with one ls-remote and no object fetches, and skips
any check already proven for the tree it is about to test — whether by an
earlier run, a re-run, or `make ci` on someone's machine. Producing one needs
push access, the same trust boundary as pushing code; forks can neither create
nor be affected by them.

Reuse is deliberately conservative because this gates a production deploy.
Checks declare the capabilities they need and attestations record the ones the
environment had, so a run that fell back to a stub service can never satisfy a
check that needs the real one. Fingerprints are pinned from the gate, so steps
that rewrite the tree (hpack, npm ci, hlint --refactor) cannot desync what gets
attested from what was looked up. The deploy condition is spelled out rather
than implied by `needs`: build-and-test may be skipped, but only when the gate
says every Haskell check was already proven.

Also switches the minio service to bitnamilegacy/minio. The bitnami/minio
repository was emptied in the Aug-2025 catalog change and now has no tags at
all; CI has only been working off a runner-side image cache, and an eviction
would have taken the integration suite down with nothing in the diff to blame.

Verified end to end: all six checks ran through ci.sh and published
attestations, and a clean checkout on macOS/arm64 then resolved CI's
linux-amd64 attestations and skipped the entire Haskell suite.

See docs/local-ci.md.

ci: stop emitting the run id twice in an attestation's provenance (#492)

Every attestation CI has published so far carries

  runner=github-run-3194584899031945848990

which is `github-run-` followed by run id 31945848990 twice, so the one
field that traces a proof back to the run that produced it cannot be
pasted into a URL.

`${X:+github-run-$X}${X:-$(whoami)@$(hostname)}` reads like an if/else and
is not one: the `:-` arm yields $X itself when X is set, so a set
GITHUB_RUN_ID takes BOTH arms. Spell the branch out.

ci: reuse an already-built image, and document running CI locally (#493)

With tests cached the deploy is 4m22s, of which 3m52s is the image build — the
whole critical path. The image is not fingerprinted like the other checks
because it produces an artifact rather than a verdict, but it does not need to
be: it is tagged with the commit SHA, so the registry is already its cache and
the SHA is already its identity.

build-image now probes the registry and skips when the tag exists. Nothing
changes for a new commit; it collapses the repeat cases to ~30 seconds — a
re-run of a failed or cancelled deploy, a workflow_dispatch of an existing
commit, a revert to an already-built SHA. Skipping re-points :latest at the
reused image rather than leaving it on an older commit, since docker-compose.yml
pulls :latest.

The same probe lets a bigger machine pre-build the image (`make deploy-image`,
linux/amd64 — Rosetta on Apple Silicon, not QEMU). That moves the artifact that
runs in production outside CI, and unlike an attestation it cannot be verified
afterwards, because a Haskell build is not bit-reproducible. So the build
refuses a dirty tree, and the deploy job prints `built by: …` every time —
never fatally, since a provenance lookup must not be why a gated build fails to
reach production.

Docs: CONTRIBUTING gains the section a contributor needs, including the two
caveats that would otherwise surprise them — the first `make ci` is a cold
build, and publishing a result needs push access, so from a fork it is fast
local feedback but CI re-runs the checks itself. README links docs/local-ci.md.

ci: one ghc-options string, so test steps stop recompiling the whole build (#495)

`build` compiled with `-O0 +RTS -A64m -n2m -RTS`; doctests, unit-tests and
cli-tests compiled with just `-O0`. cabal's build plan hash includes
ghc-options, so those are two different configurations and every test step
recompiled all ~184 modules that `build` had just compiled. That is most of
the wasted time in the job — and it was inherited from the workflow, not
introduced here.

It is also a memory cliff. Without `-A64m -n2m` GHC uses its default
allocation area, so the redundant recompile is far more GC-heavy, and on a
4-vCPU runner it dies with no error message at all — the log jumps from
"[182 of 184] Compiling …" straight to a failed step. That is exactly what
blocked the deploy of b052d6cf4: `build` passed, then `doctests` rebuilt
everything and was killed. The previous master run passed the same step,
because it had ~4.5k fewer lines to recompile.

One string everywhere. The test steps now reuse what `build` produced
instead of redoing it.

ReportUsage is the job that bills people and had no test. Six now cover the
invariants that protect customers: a free project and a paid one with no

Collapse endpoint explosion: token-level id detection, deterministic matching

One customer had 18,213 rows in apis.endpoints for ~1,900 routes, and owned
2.67M of the 7.6M rows in apis.anomalies as a direct consequence. The cause is
that isUrlIdLike matched whole segments against a list of id formats, so a
customer whose primary key is "SB-<hex>" fell through every rule: the hyphen
broke `T.all isAlphaNum`, and the vowel-ratio test misfires on hex because a-f
are hex digits. Velox (8,026) and Lunix (7,988) were next.

Classification now works on tokens. Split the percent-decoded segment on
non-alphanumeric characters and call it dynamic when any token is
machine-generated: all digits, hex with a digit, frequent digit/letter
alternation, or letters with no vowel. One rule covers prefixed ids, ids
embedded in filenames, and formats nobody has written down yet. Measured over
every endpoint row in the fleet: 50,381 -> 22,515, Shipbubble 18,248 -> 1,959,
zero idempotence violations, and of 19k segments newly called dynamic only 27
are purely alphabetic — all of them genuinely random. The rejections are
doctested as hard as the acceptances, because an earlier draft that flagged any
alphanumeric segment over 12 characters swallowed "transactions",
"subscriptions" and "notifications".

Two more general blind spots: percent-encoded ids (6,339 rows — the existing
'|' rule was written for auth0%7C… and defeated by the encoding) and router
placeholders (:id, {id}, <id>, [id]). Both are handled by parsing rather than
guessing. Decoding is for classification only and segments keep their original
text, so a %2F can never change a path's segment count.

Matching becomes deterministic. Templates are bucketed by segment count and
ordered most-literal-first, so /users/search beats /users/{param} the way an
HTTP router would, instead of whichever row Postgres aggregated first; equal
specificity is genuine ambiguity and refuses to match. Ingest now consults the
templates for paths that carry their own captured params too — it labels them
{uuid} while discovery writes {param}, and without that the same route trades
between two hashes forever: mint, merge, delete, re-mint, one new-endpoint
notification per cycle.

Discovery reduces to re-classifying and grouping. A group that matches an
existing template is assigned even at size one, which is how a straggler
arriving after the bulk merge lands on the template rather than re-inflating
the table one row at a time. Population inference is kept, gated on the
siblings sharing one character-class shape that contains a digit run, and is
report-only: without the digit requirement it proposed folding verify_phone,
deactivate_user and update_email into a single parameter.

Cleanup moves to its own job, because it is the destructive half, and it was
broken in two ways that had never surfaced — the job has never had merged pairs
to process. Its NOT EXISTS guard reads the pre-statement snapshot, so N rows
remapping onto one canonical all pass it and then collide on the unique index
(Shipbubble: 15,378 open api_change issues across 15,378 endpoints, and 18,207
endpoint anomalies); consolidation is now explicit, newest row per canonical
group wins. And no index supported LEFT(target_hash, 8), so every statement
seq-scanned a 7.6M-row table; migration 0130 adds the prefix indexes and the
statements are project-scoped and batched so they can use them.

Removes the endpoint embedding/LLM merge step, which produced zero embeddings
fleet-wide and is redundant now that grouping works.

dependency list, so the module has never compiled there. It went unnoticed
because `cabal test doctests` builds the sibling suite too, and CI's doctests
check is fingerprinted: no run since has had a reason to rebuild it, so the
attestation kept being reused. The next change to src/ was always going to
surface it.

Treat a long digit run as generated, not as part of a word

Watching the collapsed fleet, one shape kept minting fresh endpoints: a short
letter prefix on a long digit run — KWI026306565847, 14FI12032648, GAVD17082604
— tracking numbers and order references. They have a vowel, so the
consonant-soup rule passes them; the letters and digits sit in two blocks, so
the alternation ratio is far below the threshold; and a letter outside [a-f]
keeps them off the hex path. Shipbubble was still minting ~169 concrete rows an
hour through this gap, which would have undone the collapse in a few days.

Six is the cutoff because a slug's year is four ("best-restaurants-2025-guide"),
and a bare number is already a format match. Verified against every endpoint
path in the fleet: 58 additional segments classify as dynamic, none of them
alphabetic, and the existing rejections are unchanged.

Let template discovery decide which new endpoints are worth an email

A new-endpoint alert was sent from the ingest path, gated only by "this
endpoint row is less than five minutes old". Template discovery — the thing
that decides whether the row is a distinct route or an un-recognised id — ran
every six hours. So for any id format the classifier missed, the customer got
one "new endpoint detected" mail per id, each linking to an issue that was
consolidated and deleted hours later. A five-minute gate against a six-hour
learner.

Concrete paths are now deferred at ingest and announced by discovery, once it
has run over them and left them unmerged. That is a stricter test than any time
window, because it is the same decision that would otherwise have deleted the
row. Paths that are already templates cannot collapse further and still go out
immediately, so nothing that was correct before gets slower.

Discovery moves to every fifteen minutes, since its period is now the worst-case
delay on an alert. Cleanup drops to hourly: it gates nothing and it is the half
that deletes.

Independently of any of that, new-endpoint alerts are capped at ten per project
per hour, with the remainder rolled into a "+N more new endpoints" line rather
than dropped — issues over budget keep a null last_notified_at and go out on the
next pass. The correctness fixes only cover id formats we have thought of; the
cap is what bounds the cost of the next one we have not.

Catch shouty reference codes and comma-joined multi-selects

Two shapes were still each becoming their own endpoint.

SHO3KOOWWN, BUMEHU37XD, INS2UWNWIZ — a customer's order and shipment reference
format. They beat every existing rule: they carry vowels, so the consonant-soup
test passes them; they alternate twice in ten characters, well under the density
threshold; and they are not hex. The signal being ignored was the casing. Routes
are written in lower case, so all-caps alphanumeric carrying a digit is a
reference, not a word.

/v1/shipping/fetch_rates/aramex,chowdeck,dhl-nigeria,fez-delivery,... is a
multi-select rendered into the path, so every combination a caller picked became
an endpoint. This one route was 128 of that project's 551 paths — a quarter of
its apparent API surface — and none of it is an id, which is why nothing aimed
at ids was ever going to catch it.

Their own API reads as 399 distinct paths rather than 529. Checked against every
path in the fleet: 177 more segments classify as dynamic, all of them references
or courier lists, no route words among them.

Ask a small model about the endpoint groups no rule can decide

Every rule so far answers "is this segment an id", one segment at a time. What
is left over is a different question: here are eight values seen at one
position, are they eight ids or eight routes? Nothing mechanical separates
those — a template built from verify_phone/deactivate_user/update_email passes
exactly the same structural checks as one built from eight order references,
which is why the shape gate got it wrong and why a model is worth asking.

Measured against the real residual before any of this was written: 1,222 groups
fleet-wide, and on a sample weighted toward the dangerous cases the small model
was right on all of them. It merged /lnx/<00Zj,011b,01ZW> (1,262 endpoints of
four-character tokens no rule could ever justify), Microsoft Graph thread ids,
Stripe cus_ ids, hashed bundle filenames — and refused every route-word group
it was shown, including /api/<activity-logs,admin,analytics>.

Report-only. It writes to its own table and never to apis.endpoints. The
verdicts are there to be read first, because if the model is wrong in the merge
direction the cost is deleted issues and a route identity that cannot be
recovered, and no check downstream of it would notice.

Groups come from walking the trie rather than grouping on the prefix, so
mid-path families are visible; they are re-asked only when their membership
changes, so a settled project costs nothing. The shape each verdict carries
("stripe customer id", "prefixed order reference") is the real output: those
are the deterministic rules nobody has written yet, surfaced without reading
production by hand.

Not the embedding-and-judge step deleted earlier today. That one embedded every
endpoint to rediscover neighbours the classifier already knew about; this reads
only what the classifier could not decide, and answers with a verdict rather
than a merge.

Also fixes openaiSmallModel: it defaulted to gpt-5.6-luna#minimal, which that
model rejects, so every judge call — log-pattern and error-pattern merge
included — has been failing with a 400.

Review the biggest endpoint groups first

The first production run spent its budget answering questions about
three-member groups while a customer's 1,262-endpoint family of four-character
tokens sat unreviewed. Groups were taken in hash order, and the distribution is
not remotely uniform: 400 of the first 419 verdicts were small route-word
groups correctly refused, which is reassuring about precision and useless about
the backlog. Sort by member count so each run spends its calls where the
answer is worth having.

Route query-editor calls through a shim that loads Monaco first

Monaco loads lazily, armed only by pointerdown/focusin on the search box
itself. Every inline handler that called a method on <query-editor> —
facet checkboxes, saved-query rows, the field-action menu, viz tabs —
hit a still-un-upgraded element on a fresh page load and threw
"toggleSubQuery is not a function", silently dropping the filter.

window.queryEditorCall loads the chunk when the method is missing, waits
for updateComplete (firstUpdated builds the Monaco instance all those
methods bail without), then invokes. syncFacetCheckboxes falls back to
the server-rendered default-value so a reload with facets active no
longer renders every checkbox unchecked.

Put the reader back when a retention eviction cuts their anchor row

Paging history fast enough to cross the 2500-row retention window remounts
the virtualizer, and the browser clamps scrollTop to 0 for that frame. The
anchor restore is what moves the reader back — but it gave up in two cases
and left them at the top, where the load-newer sentinel (armed by the very
eviction that put them there) then fired and loaded recent rows over the
history they were reading.

Both cases are the anchor going missing: the captured row was itself in the
cut, or no anchor could be captured at all. The anchor now carries its index
in the list and mergeIntoTree records how many rows it dropped, so an
anchor-lost restore shifts that index by the cut instead of returning. When
nothing was captured, the last rendered range stands in for it.

Let a confirmed verdict merge, and let a confirmed format become a rule

Two changes that together take the human out of the loop the review step was
quietly waiting on.

A verdict may now merge, but only once four independent things agree. Two
separate passes said "param", each seeing the group among different neighbours,
because one pass is a sample of one. The group gained members between those
passes — the only signal that tells the two populations apart by behaviour
rather than appearance, since ids keep arriving forever and a family of verbs
is complete the day it ships. There are at least eight of them. And none of
them reads as a word someone would name a route after; that last test cannot
prove anything is an id, but it is sound in the refusing direction and it is
the case that has caught us out twice.

Deletion is what makes a wrong merge permanent, so cleanup now leaves
LLM-sourced merges alone for a day. Something has to look during that window
and it was never going to be a person, so the re-check asserts each merge and
asks the model to find the fault in it, rather than asking the original
question again and getting the original answer back. What it refutes is
reverted: rows restored, merge_override set so the group stops being argued
about.

The second change is what stops the model being asked the same question
forever. When a family clears the bar, the literal prefix its values share
(cus_, SB-, a-df0u-) is tested against every segment the project's own
templates treat as a route word. That test — unlike the merge decision it comes
from — has an answer, and a prefix that collides with nothing is promoted to a
deterministic rule. Rules are scoped per project and host: cus_ means Stripe
customer in one API and could mean anything in another's, and a rule learned
from one customer's traffic has no business classifying another's.

The shapes the model names are now reported hourly across the fleet. Each line
is an id format with no rule behind it yet — the two that cost an evening of
reading production this week would have been on it.

Apply what a learned id format knows, at ingest

Promoted rules were being recorded and then ignored. The prefixes a project has
been proven to use now reach the classifier: ProjectCache carries them,
PathClassifier bundles them with the templates already threaded through
ingestion, and isUrlIdLikeWith consults them before falling back to the shape
heuristics.

The doctest for it makes the case better than the comment does. A Stripe
customer id defeats every generic rule — it has vowels, it barely alternates,
it is not hex, it is not shouty — so isUrlIdLikeWith [] "cus_QpeOrF3HMRjazD" is
False and no amount of tuning the shape rules would change that without also
swallowing route words. With the project's own prefix in scope it is True,
immediately, on a path nobody has seen. That is the difference between a rule
that has to generalise across every customer and one that only has to be right
about this one.

Three test call sites passed a bare HashMap where the classifier now goes;
emptyPathClassifier is the "knows nothing about any project" value for them.

Carry the wildcard position instead of recovering it from the prefix

applyConfirmedGroups recomputed which segment a verdict was about with
`length (splitOn "/" prefix) - 1`, which is off by one for every path. The
knock-on is worse than the arithmetic: the guard that follows then matches
nothing, so the merge set is always empty and auto-apply silently does nothing
at all. It would have looked exactly like evidence still accumulating.

residualGroups already knows the position. It travels with the group now, so
there is nothing left to derive wrongly.

Alongside, from a distillation pass over the same code:

getUnmergedEndpoints was being re-read inside the per-group loop — the same
five thousand rows, once per group merged. Reviews were read twice a pass,
once for the merge and once for the promotion, each rebuilding the same
filter; confirmedGroups now derives that set once and both consume it. Inside
the row filter, `map Just kids` and an intercalate of the prefix were being
rebuilt for every candidate row, and are now a Set and a split done once.

`foldl' min maxBound` over the value lengths quietly yields maxBound on an
empty list, which would then be written to the database as a rule's minimum
length; the list is non-empty by construction, so viaNonEmpty minimum1 says
that and returns Nothing if it ever stops being true.

Seed per-project jobs again, and stop reading a default as evidence

recentlyActiveProjectIds decides which projects get per-project background
jobs, and it decided by joining projects against otel_logs_and_spans. That
table is empty in Postgres by design — telemetry moved to TimeFusion — so the
join matched nothing, the seeding loop body never ran, and no per-project job
has been created since 2026-07-17. Not endpoint discovery, not log-pattern
processing, not pattern merge, not the span-derivation safety net, and not
ReportUsage, which is the one worth looking at hardest. Nothing failed. The
jobs were simply never enqueued, which is why nothing in the queue and nothing
in the logs said so, and why 31 endpoints out of 50,957 fleet-wide had ever
been canonicalised. Activity now comes from apis.schema_catalog, which the
observation flush touches for any span at all, with anomalies as a second
source for a project whose catalog has settled.

Separately, the first auto-applied merge — Stripe account ids collapsing to
/v1/accounts/{param}, correctly — recorded its growth as 0->15. The zero was
0132's column default rather than a size anyone observed, which made
"membership grew" trivially true for every row written before the column
existed. That is the condition that separates an open set of ids from a closed
set of route names, so it is not one to hand out for free: an unrecorded
starting size is now not evidence of growth, and 0134 backfills the existing
rows to their current size so they measure from here.

Count billable events from wherever telemetry actually is

getUsageTotals routed its metrics query through the TimeFusion read flag and
left the events query hardcoded to Postgres. That was survivable until
telemetry moved and left otel_logs_and_spans empty here, at which point every
project's event count came back zero — and events are what the plans charge
for. Usage reported as nothing while usage_last_reported advanced anyway, so
each run also moved the window past the usage it had just failed to see.

Both halves follow the flag now. With reads off, behaviour is exactly what it
is today; with them on, the count comes from the store that has the rows.
TimeFusion holds 3.6M events in the last day for one project alone, against
zero in Postgres for the same query.

No change to the cycle-start cap: the next run reports from the start of each
project's current billing cycle, not from the stale watermark, so nothing is
charged for cycles that have already closed.

Count usage in day slices, bounded by the recorded window end

A whole billing cycle in one aggregate exceeds TimeFusion's 60s statement
timeout for high-volume projects, and a timeout there fails the entire
usage report. DSI-APP writes ~33M metric rows a day, so its otel_metrics
aggregate never completed: job 37854019 exhausted all 10 attempts on
"canceling statement due to statement timeout" and the project has not
reported since 2026-07-17.

Split the window into contiguous one-day slices and sum them. Verified
against production TimeFusion: for DSI-APP over 2026-08-01..08-24 the
single-shot and 23-slice totals agree exactly on both count and bytes
(39633 | 94497674). A single day runs in ~20s, so the full pass fits well
under the 600s odd-jobs timeout.

Also bound the count above by the window end the caller records. It was
open-ended, so rows arriving between nowU and query execution were counted
in this window and again in the next one, which starts at nowU.

Render the issue page when its trace won't load in time

The trace behind an issue is supporting evidence, not the page. A cold
TimeFusion read of a 1300-span trace took 56s on
issues/071ba0c6-9144-458e-bc3d-1d449630131e, so the gateway 504'd the
whole page — stack trace, error details, chart and logs included.

Budget the fetch (TRACE_VIEW_TIMEOUT_SECS, 20s) and isolate its failures.
Past the budget, or on a read error, the Investigation pane alone
degrades and says so; everything else renders. TracePane keeps that state
distinct from "this issue never had a trace", which the old empty state
would have claimed.

Load an issue's trace as its own fragment, not as part of the page

Fetching the waterfall inline meant the whole issue page waited on the
single slowest read it makes. The Investigation panel now pulls the
existing /p/:pid/traces/:id fragment over HTMX, so the stack trace, error
details, chart and logs render immediately and the waterfall arrives when
it arrives.

The budget moves down with it: traceH bounds its own fetch, which also
covers the standalone trace page, and answers with a retryable state
instead of hanging past the gateway. That state now carries the URL that
produced it — Retry re-issues the same request in place, where before it
sent an event only the log explorer listened for, and silently did
nothing anywhere else.

Everything the page still wanted from those 1300 spans is resolved
without them: the session id by a scalar lookup, the trace id for the
logs tab from the reference we already had, and the user journey inside
the activity fragment that was already loading lazily beside it.

Point trace Retry at the fallback, not at the row of buttons

`closest div` from the Retry button is the flex row holding it, so a
retry would have swapped the two buttons out for a whole trace view and
left the failure copy standing above it.

Pin the trace reference the activity fragment carries

The user journey now arrives through /activity, so losing ?trace_id and
&trace_ts from that URL would empty it with every other assertion in the
suite still green. The fixture gains real issue_data too — without it the
RuntimeException branch renders nothing, so the assertion was checking a
panel that was never on the page.

Fetch a trace a page at a time, with the next page on request

A trace view pulled every span it could find. On a 1300-span trace that
is 4.4MB of HTML and ~8s of browser parse, and nothing bounded how much
worse it could get.

The fetch now takes the first N spans by start time (300 by default,
?spans= to ask for more) and reports whether the trace continues. When it
does, the view says so — "300+" spans, and a control that reloads it at
double the size. Each pull is one bounded request, so no single view can
be arbitrarily large.

Reloading the whole view rather than appending is deliberate: the
waterfall is a tree, and a later page's spans belong under earlier pages'
parents. Orphan-parent resolution is skipped while a page is truncated,
where "missing" mostly means "not fetched yet" and chasing it would pull
back exactly the rows the page limit exists to avoid.

Note this bounds transfer and render, not TimeFusion's scan: a count over
this trace costs about as much as the full read, so the cold-read tail is
addressed by the fragment's budget, not by the page size.

Keep span lookup and the first-span anchor out of the page limit

Two things the paging change got wrong.

Nav looks a span up by id rather than drawing the trace, so capping it at
the render page meant a click on span #301 of a 1300-span trace found
nothing and silently opened the root instead — a wrong answer, not a slow
one. It takes the clamp maximum now.

And a Load more swap carries the whole fragment with it, auto-open marker
included, so every pull dragged the detail panel back to the first span.
The marker is emitted on the first load only.

Both are pinned by assertions on a 60-span trace; the existing nav test
uses three spans, which is why neither showed up.

comparison says unchanged and the job completes having done nothing. Nothing

Defer RUM and Infrastructure page bodies past first paint

Every Infrastructure view (hosts, containers, images, kubernetes, host map)
blocked its first byte on the same multi-second metrics pivot, and RUM blocked
on up to seven concurrent 24-hour scans. Clicking between tabs meant a blank
page for as long as the slowest query took.

The first request now renders chrome plus a skeleton and touches no store; the
body arrives on the follow-up request the skeleton fires, swapped in place so
nav, tabs and the time picker are never re-rendered. Filters ride the round
trip, so the rows that arrive are the rows the visible filter chips claim.

The host and container drawers also re-ran the snapshot query against a default
window rather than the one the row was rendered from — they now carry the
page's window, which both fixes the numbers and lets the read be reused.

Mark the deferred shell so tests wait for the real body

A skeleton satisfies a visibility check as readily as content does. The
cursor audit and the host map's control-size loop both looked at whatever
had arrived after a fixed 500ms, which after deferral is the skeleton — they
would have kept passing while checking nothing.

Pin the deferred contract in the page specs

Asserts the first request carries chrome, a self-fetching skeleton and the
filters it was asked for, and carries no rows — the property that breaks if
the deferral is undone. Reaching for the body now names the failure when a
handler answers with a shell instead of crashing on a partial pattern.

Also drops a duplicate rum-page id: the shell wrapper already supplies it.

Scope RUM to one browser service, and stop double-encoding panel links

Two things a project with several teams runs into.

The page averaged every browser service in the project together, with no way
to narrow it — a checkout regression hidden behind a healthy marketing site.
Every read now shares one scope definition rather than repeating the same four
WHERE lines six times, so the service filter is a single predicate the summary,
trend, tables and vitals cannot disagree about. The picker offers only services
that actually emit browser telemetry: a backend service in a RUM picker scopes
the page to something that can never have a page view.

The Log Explorer links shipped their KQL URI-encoded, and windowUrl encodes
every value it is given — so a space arrived as %2520 and the Explorer parsed
the whole query as one meaningless token. Nothing pre-encodes now. The scope
rides those links too, as a KQL clause, so what the Explorer lists is what the
panel counted.

The pid/window pair every self-link took is now one RumLinks value, so a new
scope dimension cannot be added to the handler and forgotten by half the links.
Recordings carry no service, so under a scope they attach to sessions a span
already places in that service rather than adding rows of their own.

Don't tell a scoped-to-nothing RUM page to install the browser SDK

A service filter that matched nothing is not an uninstrumented project, but it
reached the same empty state — telling a user with working telemetry to
re-instrument a working app. Reachable via the picker, which deliberately keeps
offering a selection whose data has aged out of the window. The scoped state
names the service and offers the way out: widen back to all services.

Make RUM see the browser telemetry it was filtering out

The service picker had nothing to offer because RUM had nothing to show. Every
RUM query narrowed on resource.telemetry.sdk.language IN ('webjs','javascript',
'js'), and nothing in production sets it: a platform-wide scan over 90 minutes
returns zero rows for all three values. Meanwhile three browser applications
were reporting the whole time - frontend-web, talstack-web, monoscope-ui - so
the page was scoped to the empty set and the picker, which lists the services
it finds, correctly rendered nothing.

Browser telemetry is now identified by a ladder of what browsers actually send:
the sdk language when present, the browser resource detector's user agent, the
OpenTelemetry browser instrumentation span names, and our own SDK's page-view
naming. resourceFetch is deliberately excluded - one span per script, stylesheet
and image, 40% of all browser rows, carrying nothing RUM displays.

Two things followed from the same mistake:

- Page views were counted as name LIKE 'Pageview . %', which is our SDK's
  naming only. documentLoad is the OpenTelemetry browser SDK's page load, so
  the count is now a shared predicate both shapes go through.
- Page identity read attributes.url.path, which the browser SDK leaves null
  while setting url.full. Every Top Pages row would have collapsed onto one
  blank path. Same fallback now applies to session last-page and error rows.

The Explore links carried the dead filter too, so they opened an Explorer view
of nothing; they now use the KQL counterpart of the same ladder.

Panels run concurrently again rather than two at a time. That batching was
introduced on the finding that TimeFusion degrades when they compete, but it
was measured while every query matched zero rows. Re-measured against real
data, four concurrent scans take 7.4s and the same four in two batches take
8.1s.

13 examples, 0 failures. The new one ingests a page load shaped exactly as the
OpenTelemetry browser SDK sends it - documentLoad, url.full, a resource user
agent, no sdk.language - and asserts it is both visible and narrowable.

Size cache entries to the window they cover, not to one flat 15s

A cache whose entries expire before the page that fills them has finished
building is worse than none: it pays every write and serves no read. Both
telemetry caches were set to a flat 15s while the work they cache takes far
longer. Measured on the demo project: RUM over 24h assembles in 24s, and the
infrastructure snapshot takes 0.4s over five minutes but 32-60s over a day. So
at the windows that hurt, not one entry was ever reused.

A flat larger number is wrong at the other end - five minutes of staleness is
0.3% of a 24-hour count and invisible, but it is the whole of a five-minute
one. TimePicker.cacheTtl makes the budget a fraction of the window instead,
floored at 30s so an entry outlives the page that produced it, and capped at
the 300s the sibling host and endpoint stats caches already allow. Data.Cache
insert' takes a relative TTL per entry, so no new machinery is needed.

Measured after: RUM at 24h 24.2s -> 2.2s on the second visit; infrastructure
hosts at 1h 2.2s -> 0.4s.

Separately, and not fixed here: the infrastructure snapshot query does not
merely get slow over a 24h window, it fails. TimeFusion exhausts its whole
16 GB memory pool spilling through ExternalSorter and the page returns a 500.
That is pre-existing - the pivot is untouched by this branch - but it means a
user selecting a day on the Hosts page can degrade a shared service for
everyone, and it deserves its own fix.

fix(kql): validate metrics queries against the metrics schema, not nothing

`unknownField` skipped field validation entirely for `source=metrics`, so a
metrics widget shipped spans-only columns straight to TimeFusion:

  select ..., coalesce(status_code::text, ?) from otel_metrics
  where ... and ((level = ?)) ...
  -> Schema error: No field named level. Valid fields are otel_metrics.timestamp, ...

TF answers that for the WHOLE query, so the widget renders empty with a wall of
column names. The skip was there for a real reason — metrics read a different
table, and checking `metric_name`/`value` against otel_logs_and_spans rejected
the metrics table's own columns — but the fix for "wrong column set" was a
second column set, not the absence of one.

`FieldUniverse` is that set: bare columns plus the dotted flattened ones, one
per queryable table. `unknownField` picks by source, and both universes are
seeded from `information_schema` at startup the way spans already were
(`setMetricsColumns` alongside `setOtelColumns`), so a schema change widens
them without a code change; the hand-coded builtins remain the fallback.

Aliases now resolve per-universe rather than unconditionally: `Display Subject`
rewrites `trace_id` to `context___trace_id` no matter the table, so on metrics
that alias names a column that does not exist and is rejected here instead.
`service` and `method` survive on both — their targets exist on both tables.

The check stays deliberately narrow: it looks at the subject ROOT, so every
`attributes.*`/`resource.*` path still passes on the `attributes`/`resource`
root, and only bare spans-only roots (`level`, `status_code`, `duration`,
`span_name`, `trace_id`) are rejected. The failure users see becomes the
widget's own "Unknown field" overlay via the existing `withChartSpan` path.

Also: raise the TimeFusion postgresql-simple pool's idle TTL 30s -> 1800s, to
match the hasql pools. At 30s a chart-heavy page reopened TF connections
continuously and connect() returned EADDRNOTAVAIL under widgetGetH ->
processEagerWidget -> fetchMetricsData. One occurrence, so this is a contributor
rather than a proven cause; no test is constructible for a pool-config value.

fix(ui): adopt time transports whose on-load hook ran before the bundle

Three "'window.initTimeTransport' is null" criticals on 2026-08-28. The
web-components bundle is a deferred module, so a `[data-time-transport]`
rendered above it fires `on load call window.initTimeTransport(me)` before that
assignment exists. The hook throws, and the transport is left uninitialised —
the dashboard the user believes is live never refreshes.

Guarding the hyperscript alone would only trade the error for silence, so
main.ts adopts any transport that missed the call, keyed on `dataset.live` —
the marker `initTimeTransport` itself sets, so a transport that DID reach the
hook is never initialised twice. Adoption runs at parse time and on
`htmx:after:swap`, which also covers a swap that re-renders the transport
without re-running its hook.

The test drives the swap path (the one reachable from jsdom) and pins both
halves: an unadopted transport starts its timer, and a second swap does not
restart or double it. It fails without the adoption call.

fix(kql): a post-summarize filter on a raw column is a WHERE, not a HAVING

`markPostSummarizeFilters` re-tagged EVERY filter after a summarize as a
HavingClause. On an aggregate output that is right; on a raw column it emitted

  … GROUP BY time_bucket(?, timestamp), … HAVING (metric_name = ?)

— a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated, which the backend rejects,
losing the whole query rather than the one clause.

Filtering a raw column before the aggregate is the same answer and is always
valid SQL, so those conjuncts now become a WhereClause that `reorderSections`
already hoists above the summarize. Conjuncts are split first because one query
mixes both kinds (`| where metric_name == "x" and count_ > 5`), and the test
for "is this an aggregate output" is the summarize's own `definedNames` — which
is why `go` now carries the SummarizeCommand instead of a Bool.

An `Or` spanning both kinds stays a HavingClause: it cannot be evaluated in
either place alone, and it is rare enough not to earn rejection machinery.

Doctests pin all three shapes — raw column to WHERE, alias to HAVING, and the
mixed conjunction splitting one each way.

fix(kql): reject a bin() width we cannot bucket by, instead of silently using 5m

`kqlTimespanToTimeBucket` ended in `fromMaybe "5 minutes"`, so every width it
failed to parse became five minutes with no error anywhere. Measured on prod
against a fixed one-hour window, by row count:

  bin(timestamp, 30sec)  -> 5-minute buckets   (asked for 30 seconds)
  bin(timestamp, 10min)  -> 5-minute buckets   (asked for 10 minutes)
  bin(timestamp, 1mo/1M/1y/2wk) -> 5-minute buckets

The chart answered a different question than the one asked, and said nothing.
`5min` "worked" only by coincidence. Anyone arriving from Grafana or PromQL,
where `10min` and `1M` are ordinary, got a wrong chart silently.

It now returns Maybe, and `unsupportedTimespan` turns the Nothing into a
positioned parse error alongside the existing unknown-field diagnostics, so the
editor squiggles the width and names the spelling to use. `defaultBinWidth` is
a named constant because the fallback being an inline "5 minutes" is precisely
what kept this invisible; the two render sites keep it only for callers that
skip validation, and both say so.

DELIBERATELY NOT WIDENED: accepting sec/min/hr/wk was implemented and reverted.
The function rendered them correctly — the doctests prove "30sec" -> Just
"30 seconds" — but end to end the query still bucketed at one minute, and
10min at roughly five. Whatever mangles them between here and the SQL was not
found, and shipping an alias that buckets wrong while PASSING validation is
strictly worse than the bug being fixed. `timespanSuffixes` records the
measurement and requires an end-to-end row-count check before any re-add; a
green doctest is what misled the first attempt.

Verified on the running app: 30s/1m/10m/1h give 120/60/6/1 rows over a fixed

— the silent fallback, written down as the expected result. My push left CI red
because I ran doctests and an end-to-end check but not `make test-unit`.

A bare number is SECONDS. The shipped README is the evidence:

  method == "GET" | summarize count(*) by bin(timestamp, 86400)

Blast radius is small and all of it corrective. `bin(timestamp, 300)` — the form

fix(log explorer): a live update no longer throws a scrolled reader to the top

Reported as "scrolling down, I get pushed back to the latest logs, usually after
the 15 second live update". Traced in the browser, the chain was:

Retention was a single threshold that one page of history overshot on arrival,
so every load-more evicted, and every eviction remounts the virtualizer through
keyed(). 76s of scrolling produced 17 remounts. A remount blanks the runway, so
the browser clamps scrollTop to 0 — and fires a scroll event for that clamp.
resumeLiveTailAtEdge read that as "the reader came back to the newest edge" and
flushed the whole buffered tick into someone deep in history, which evicted the
history they were reading and left them at the top on the newest rows.

So: resumeLiveTailAtEdge now stands down while repositioning, as syncBottomPin
and the proximity prefetch already did — a frame of collapsed geometry is not
the reader's intent. And retention became a pair (cross RETENTION_LIMIT, cut
back to MAX_RETAINED_ROWS) so a cut is rare instead of once per page.

80s of continuous scrolling across several real ticks: 4 remounts, no
unexplained scroll losses, buffered rows held rather than flushed.

Off the scroll path as well: healBlankVirtualizer is a last-resort watchdog, but
it ran on every render and measured every mounted row, which was the largest
app-level cost in a CPU profile of a throttled scroll. It now runs only off its
timers, and is O(1) — mounted rows are one contiguous band, so the first and
last bound the rest. The buffer flush is coalesced into one rAF, and the
virtualizer layout specifier is hoisted instead of reallocated per render.

The scroll harness simulated the remount's scrollTop=0 clamp but never fired the
scroll event the browser fires with it, which is why no test caught this. It
does now, and both regressions fail without their fix.

perf(infra): read the container pivot from a freshness slice, not the whole window

Over a 24-hour window the containers query did not complete at all — it hit the
statement timeout, so `containersInWindowCached` never got a value to store, the
300s TTL never applied, and every load paid the full timeout and rendered
nothing. Measured on prod TF against the demo project: 1.77s at 1h, 42.33s at
6h, timeout at 24h.

The window was the wrong input. The values shown are by definition the newest
datapoint per series, and a series that still exists reports every 15-60s, so
its newest datapoint is always within the last few minutes. Scanning further
back can only turn up older points that `rn = 1` then discards — while paying to
sort every one of them, with ~15 variant_get lookups per row along the way.

So the pivot now reads `[max(fromTime, toTime - 15m), toTime]`. Anchored on the
window's end rather than on `now`, so a historical from/to range reports the
state at the end of the range it selected, and a window shorter than the slice
still only reads itself. Result: 0.70s flat at every window — 63x at 6h, and 24h
goes from not completing to sub-second.

That drops a container which stopped reporting hours ago off a wide window,
instead of showing it with hours-old numbers sorted among the live ones by CPU.
That is the intended reading of the table, and keeping the old semantics is not
affordable: a presence-only query over the window costs 8.77s at 6h and 25.12s
at 24h, because the scan is the expense, not the pivot. The result summary now
says "reporting in the last 15m" rather than implying the picker's window.

Also fixes the two usage charts above the table, which rendered as empty panels.
They sized themselves purely by `aspect-ratio: 4/1`, so side by side on a 1600px
viewport each canvas got 56px — no plot area for a multi-series line chart with a
legend, even though both /chart_data requests returned full datasets. A height
floor takes the canvas to 140px; the ratio still governs growth on wide screens.

fix(tables): scroll wide tables horizontally instead of clipping their columns

The table grid wrapper was `overflow-hidden`, so any table wider than its
content area simply lost the overflow — no scrollbar, no way to reach it.
Measured at 1600x1000 with the facet rail open: Containers needs 1460px and gets
1250, Kubernetes needs 1819, Images 1784. Between 210 and 569 pixels of columns
were unreachable on the infrastructure pages.

Only the x axis changes. The reason this looked risky is that `overflow-x: auto`
makes the browser compute `overflow-y: auto` when y is `visible`, which would
turn the div into a scroll container and steal the sticky thead's scroll root.
That does not apply here: `overflow-hidden` had already set `overflow-y: hidden`,
so the box was a scroll container in both axes before this change and still is,
and the computed overflow-y is `hidden` either way. Checked in the browser
before changing it — with x set to auto, scrollLeft reaches the full 210px that
was previously unreachable, and the header's resolved position is unchanged.

Every table renders through this component, and the change moves them all in the
same direction: one that fits is untouched, one that does not now scrolls rather

fix(widgets): render a raw-SQL widget's columns whatever their type

The DTText path decoded every column as Text, and postgresql-simple's
FromField Text rejects anything else — so one uncast column failed the *whole*

and the author got an error overlay instead of their table. Widget SQL is
hand-written, so requiring ::text on every column was a trap rather than a
contract. The reported case was date_part(EPOCH, time_bucket(...)), which comes
back float8.

requests results in text format: the bytes handed to fromField are already the
rendering ::text would have produced. Decoded with lenientDecode — a decode
error here would only trade one whole-widget failure for another.

throwing UnexpectedNull and killing the widget.

fix(auth): answer a fetch with 401, not a redirect to an HTML login page

A fetch follows a 302 transparently, so redirecting an unauthenticated XHR to
/login hands JavaScript a 200 HTML document and every res.json() in the app
throws `Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "`. res.ok is true, so no client-side
guard can catch it. That is what has been paging once an hour for 133 days:
a tab whose session expired repaints "Couldn't load this chart" on every
refresh tick and never recovers, because nothing tells it to re-authenticate.

challengeFor classifies the request and replies in the protocol it speaks:
basic-auth 401 as before, HX-Redirect for an htmx swap (a 302 makes htmx
inline the login page into whichever fragment asked), 401 JSON for fetch/XHR,
and the old 302 for a navigation or a client too old to send Sec-Fetch-Mode.
widgets.ts sends Accept: application/json and reloads on 401.

Also escapes redirect_to. escapedQueryPartial leaves `&` alone, so
`redirect_to=/chart_data?pid=…&since=1H` truncated at the `&` and post-login
landed on a URL missing every parameter after the first.

Three tests verified red first (expected: 401, but got: 302). The plan doc
records the triage of the other alert named alongside this one: every
occurrence of the HasqlException comes from service.name=monoscope-dev — local
dev servers write ~475k spans/day into the production self-telemetry project
and can page the team for errors that only exist on a laptop.

feat(endpoints): treat http.route as the route, in every framework's spelling

http.route is the one place a path template arrives as fact rather than
inference — the router matched the request against it. We already preferred it
over url.path, and then handed it, in the framework's own syntax, to code that
expects a URL. What reached the product was the syntax:

- 673 endpoints across 3 projects ending in a regex "$"
- 1,378 with no leading slash
- 162 truncated mid-pattern, because Django writes "(?P<pk>[^/.]+)" and
  normalizeUrlPath strips a URL's query string at the first "?"
- 1,540 carrying ":name" across 13 projects, never recognised as parameters

normalizeHttpRoute reads the syntaxes SDKs actually send — Django named groups
and anchors, Express/Gin/Rails ":name", ASP.NET/Laravel/Spring "{name}" with
constraints and catch-alls, Flask "<int:name>", Go 1.22 "{name...}" — and emits
one shape: leading slash, no anchors, plain {name}. The named-group rewrite runs
before any split on "/", because the character class contains a slash; splitting
first is what produced "api/v1/wallets/(".

A route carrying a parameter is authority, so it skips the id heuristics
entirely, and a new one is written as its own canonical template. That reuses
machinery rather than adding a column: discovery only reads canonical_hash IS
NULL, so it can never merge a router's own route away; cleanup only deletes
rows where hash != canonical_hash; and the project cache collects canonical_path,
so a service reporting only url.path resolves onto the template a *different*
service declared. One instrumented framework teaches the project its routes.

Two guards. A catch-all with no literal segment ("/{path}") is refused, or it
would swallow every path of its length. And adopting framework parameter names
renames endpoints — a rename is a new hash — so the named form only wins where
the project has nothing already; an existing row under either spelling keeps its
hash instead of the 13 affected projects re-minting and re-notifying wholesale.

The legacy SDK bridge synthesises http.route from the raw URL. It carries no
parameter, so it is not authority and nothing about its handling changes.

perf(metrics): define the datapoints table's repeated icons once

63,763 tags. 904 KB of that was SVG, of which only 17 KB was distinct — three
badge icons in the "Referenced in" column plus the tree chevron, inlined again

faSprite_ inlines an icon's paths at each call site, which is right for a page
that shows an icon once and wrong for a table. faSymbolDefs_/faUse_ are the pair
for the table case: define each icon once as a <symbol>, reference it per row.

Same-document <use>, not the sprite file — a reference into another document
renders in a shadow tree the page's CSS cannot reach, which is exactly what
.icon { fill: currentColor } needs. The <g> holding the symbol's own
presentation attributes stays inside the symbol, for the same reason faSprite_
keeps it inside the <svg>.

904 KB -> 221 KB, 1,843 <use> against 4 <symbol>. Every <use> target resolves and
the viewBoxes are preserved.

is the next thing to fix there. This is the part that could be fixed without
changing what the page shows.

perf(issues): reach the prefix index in the acknowledge cascade

Scoping to the project took the issues sweep from a sequential scan to an index
scan, but left anomalies on a bitmap scan filtered by the LIKE — a LIKE against a
parameter array is not sargable, and apis.anomalies is 6.29M rows.

Migration 0130 already built the index this needs, on both tables:
(project_id, LEFT(target_hash, 8)) — added for the endpoint-merge cleanup, which
hit the same Seq Scan for the same reason. So the sweep now narrows on that
expression and keeps the LIKE as the exact test. No migration, no semantic
change.

  issues     Seq Scan 11,438  ->  +project_id  375   ->  +prefix index   2.64
  anomalies  Seq Scan 224,708 ->  +project_id ~170k  ->  +prefix index  41.66

The narrowing is only a valid superset while every target is at least the 8
characters the index is built on: for a shorter target LEFT(row, 8) is longer
than the target itself and the filter would drop rows the LIKE would have
matched. Hence the guard, and a test for exactly that case — this function also
sweeps legacy hashes and must not quietly stop finding them.

`COUNT(*) * 100.0 / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER ()` answers 33 on TimeFusion where
Postgres gives 33.333, so endpoint-stats' status-code breakdown rendered 33 and
16 and the column did not add up to 100.

The trigger is the WINDOW aggregate in the divisor, not integer arithmetic in
general: the same shape over a plain `GREATEST(1, COUNT(*))` divisor is exact,
which is why the uncast error-rate widgets across `_overview.yaml` are fine and
were left alone. `OVER ()` appears exactly once in the dashboards, so this is
the only affected site. Casting the operands to ::float avoids it; the trailing
::float is load-bearing too, because `ROUND(<numeric>, 1)::text` renders
"33.3000000000" there — the numeric does not carry its scale.

Both the bug and this spelling are pinned in TimeFusion's
monoscope_query_shapes.slt (13b, 13c), with 13d as the counter-example that
bounds the blast radius. The regression guard lives there rather than here
because the assertion needs a TimeFusion engine to mean anything.

Also corrects three comments that describe TimeFusion defects since fixed, each
still being read as a live constraint:

- the `Utf8View` OR predicate returning wrong rows (ServiceGraph, Containers).
  Fixed by TF e0bf291, and the cause was never Utf8View — the tantivy
  id-prefilter intersects per-term id sets, sound for AND and empty for OR.
  `IN` stays on both, but as a speed choice now rather than a correctness one.
- "FIRST_VALUE is a window function and errors without OVER on both" — true of
  Postgres, not of DataFusion.
- the COALESCE(hashes, '{}') 500, fixed upstream; the projection stays bare
  because the Maybe on 'hashes' already absorbs NULL from legacy PG rows.

fix(log explorer): the load-more cursor skipped up to 999us of rows per page

The page predicate is inclusive -- `timestamp <= cursor` (Pkg/Parser.hs:84) -- so
a cursor must be nudged off the boundary or the last row of a page reappears as
the first row of the next. The two paths that do this had drifted:

  LogQueries: +0.000001  (1us)   -- recent/newer window
  Log.hs:934: -0.001     (1ms)   -- load-more cursor

The opposite signs are correct: one pages backwards, the other forward. The
magnitude is not. One microsecond is the smallest step that clears an inclusive
bound; a millisecond discards every row in the gap. A project writing thousands
of rows per millisecond -- which is the normal case for the log explorer -- lost
rows between pages, invisibly, because each page looked complete on its own.

Both paths now share one `cursorEpsilon` and one doctested `nudgeCursorBy`, so
the two can't drift again, and the doctests pin the microsecond step in both
directions plus the unparseable-input case.

fix(security): archiveAnomaliesAndIssues took no project id — a cross-tenant write

This is an IDOR *write*, not a read. `archiveAnomaliesAndIssues` had no ProjectId
parameter at all, and both of its statements were exposed:

  UPDATE apis.issues … WHERE id = ANY(?)

whose ids come straight off the bulk-action form in Pages/Anomalies.hs, so any
authenticated tenant could archive any issue in the database by submitting its id;
and the cascade

  UPDATE apis.anomalies … WHERE target_hash IN (related)

keyed on target_hash, which is content-derived and therefore *collides across
projects* — the file's own acknowlegeCascade haddock documents that collision.
So the blast radius was not limited to ids the attacker knew.

`acknowledgeAnomalies` had the same shape half-fixed: its anomalies cascade was
scoped but the issues UPDATE and its CTE were not, despite pid already being a
parameter. Three further inline statements in Pages/Anomalies.hs updated
apis.issues / apis.anomalies by URL-supplied id with no project filter.

All scoped. Guarded by archiveAnomaliesAndIssues_crossTenant_archivesOnlyTheCallersProject,
which puts two projects on one shared target_hash and submits both ids together
exactly as a tampered bulk form would, then asserts only the caller's rows moved.

That is the third cross-tenant defect this sweep — after the monitors bulk actions
and selectIssueById — and the pattern is identical every time: a function that
takes ids but not the tenant. Worth a targeted audit of every remaining
`WHERE id = ANY(...)` that has no project predicate.

decodeEnumSC so it cannot drift from the WrappedEnumSC encoding.

fix(monitors): PATCH left the compiled SQL stale, so alerts ran the old query

log_query_as_sql is the compiled form that alert evaluation actually executes.
apiMonitorPatch built its merged monitor from the stored row, so patching `query`
updated log_query and inherited the previous compiled SQL — the monitor went on
alerting against the query the user had just replaced. PUT and apply recompute it
via monitorFromInput; PATCH never did.

The failing test showed it exactly: after patching to `status_code == 500`, the
stored SQL still read `((status_code = 200))`.

The compilation is now one shared compileAlertSql used by both paths, rather than a
second copy in the patch handler. It keeps the existing fallback semantics — an
unparseable query leaves the previous compiled SQL in place, so a bad edit cannot
blank it — and PATCH recompiles whenever either the query or its time window moves,
since the window is baked into the compiled form.

`active` flag and the git-sync path prefix.

fix(errors): stop the fingerprint shattering on any hex run of an odd length

`hexDigest` recognised only 64/40/32/24 (sha256/sha1/md5/uuid). Every other hex
run fell through to `integerFb`, which emitted `{integer}` for the leading digits
and rescanned the letters — so `SB-3FDBA2D0A0A2` and `SB-90770E7BA9FD` normalised
to DIFFERENT strings. Every order id became its own error group, its own issue
row, and its own notification, which is the "we keep getting told about errors
we have seen before" report.

Measured over 30 days of prod error_patterns: 1486 distinct hashes where 783 is
right. One group alone — the same `insert into orders` failure — was 178.

12 as the floor, not 8: at 8 this starts eating short commit SHAs and hex-looking
words that are the only thing telling two errors apart, and the corpus says that
reach is worth 13 groups (770 vs 783). 16 leaves the 12-15 char ids that dominate
the fan-out (1134).

Over-merge checked against the corpus, not assumed: the groups this newly merges
are one bug each — `SB-{hex} not processing` x117, a single TLS handshake failure
x65 — while genuinely different conditions (`already cancelled` vs `already
completed`) stay apart.

This changes fingerprints, so every currently-open pattern mints a new hash on its
next occurrence: expect one final duplication wave as the corrected groups form.

  spike detection minted fresh issues and alerts for merged rows.
- the `UORegressed` branch — consulted neither, so a pattern merged while resolved
  minted a brand new issue the moment it recurred.

The asymmetry is what made this invisible: rows pre-merged at ingest never get an
issue, so the sweep's `JOIN i.target_hash = e.hash` excludes them. Only rows merged
AFTER their issue existed leak — which is every row a post-hoc merge produces, so
merging errors changed nothing a user would notice.

Also: `parseGroupReview` now drops any key answered twice instead of leaving the
caller to `HM.fromList` (last-wins). The prompt lists every key in the batch and
the reviewed text is written by whoever sent us the error, so a second line naming
a sibling key could overwrite that sibling's real verdict. A dropped key is simply
re-asked next pass.

feat(errors): give error patterns a shape key that survives a re-fingerprint

`shape` is error type plus normalised message and nothing else — no service, no
span name, no stack. It is deliberately coarser than the fingerprint and is NOT
one: same shape with different stack traces is two bugs by `narrow`'s own
definition, and the haddock says so, because the tempting misuse is to suppress on
it directly.

It exists so a review — and the merge a review authorises — survives a change to
the fingerprint. The hex fix just re-keyed every open pattern; anything keyed on
`hash` would have been orphaned by that wave, while a shape is computed from
content a re-hash does not change.

A new column rather than a reuse of `parent_hash`: that one holds broad-hash values
on all 23,372 existing rows and is refreshed only on resolve, so reading it as a
shape would match wrong rows, silently, and worst during exactly the wave this is
meant to survive.

No backfill migration — the shape is a Haskell normalisation with no SQL
equivalent. The upsert fills it with COALESCE, so a row takes its shape the next
time it occurs and never pays a rewrite after that; unconditional assignment would
rewrite a column per occurrence on the hottest path in the product, which is the
churn `recent_trace_id` is already throttled to avoid. Rows that never recur do not
need one — there is nothing left for them to suppress.

feat(errors): review error groups by shape, refute the proposals, merge survivors

Ports the endpoint loop — propose, gate on evidence, apply, quarantine, challenge,
revert — to errors, which is where the notifications people actually complain
about come from.

Deliberately NOT the embedding path. `patternEmbeddingAndMerge` has produced zero
vectors across 23,372 error patterns and 4,071,862 log patterns since it was
written, and the headroom here is lexical anyway: 427 singleton `Error` groups
share 162 openings, and 11 `SomeAsyncException` groups share exactly one. Shape
clustering reaches that for free without depending on a tier nobody has seen work.

Three things this does that the endpoint loop does not:

- Refutes before applying, not only in quarantine. A third pass is asked to find
  the fault in each proposal, and `errorGroupEvidenceMet` requires it to have
  failed. Agreeing twice with the same question is largely the model agreeing with
  itself; surviving the opposite question is worth more. A failed refutation call
  leaves proposals ineligible rather than unrefuted-therefore-fine.
- Keeps a mechanical veto the author of an error message cannot argue with.
  Confirmations and the refutation both re-read the same attacker-supplied text on
  every pass, so `errorCanMerge` gates the apply without asking the model anything.
- Sweeps the whole corpus on a cursor that restarts at the end, rather than only
  looking at new rows. The cursor advances over everything examined, not just what
  was asked about, or a skipped prefix is re-walked forever — and it restarts
  rather than stopping, because a shape that gains members later deserves another
  look. `replay_merge_succeeds_without_merging` is what the other choice looks like.

Thresholds are looser than the endpoint ones on purpose: a wrong endpoint merge
deletes issues irreversibly, a wrong error merge sets a column `revertErrorGroupApply`
clears. Auto-apply defaults OFF so the first deploy records verdicts and
refutations without acting on them.

Only normalised messages reach the prompt — placeholders already substituted for
ids, hex, timestamps and emails. Raw error text is whatever a customer's code put
in it, and this is a vendor call.

Smoke-tested the loop on prod by enqueueing one job by hand — the daily seeding

walked the corpus, it advanced its cursor, and it recorded zero verdicts.

types(issues): collapse issueType + issueData into one IssuePayload sum

`MkIssueOpts` carried `issueType :: IssueType` beside `issueData :: a`, so any
writer could pair a QueryAlert tag with LogPatternData and the compiler was fine
with it. Readers then had to guess: eight `case issue.issueType of … withIssueDataH
@SomeData issue.issueData` ladders, plus three ad-hoc `AE.fromJSON` pairings in
three different modules, each restating the tag→type mapping by hand.

columns via `payloadType`/`payloadJson`. The mismatch is unconstructible at all

GHC checks exhaustiveness — a sixth IssueType breaks the build instead of falling
through silently. `payloadType` is deliberately wildcard-free for the same reason.
`withIssueDataH` and the ad-hoc pairings in Anomalies/ApiHandlers are gone.

The wire format is unchanged, and that is load-bearing rather than incidental:
SQL reads inside this object (issue_data->>'anomaly_hashes') and *merges* into it
with `jsonb ||` at two writers. A derived sum encoding would nest the fields a
level deeper, so those merges would write keys at the wrong depth and every
existing row would stop parsing. So `payloadJson`/`parsePayload` are explicit
per-arm delegations to the existing DAE.Snake instances and there is deliberately
NO To/FromJSON instance on the sum. The Haddock says so, so a future "just derive
it" cleanup trips over it.

- `issuePayload` returns Maybe because rows exist with no issue_data at all
  (EndpointDiscoverySpec inserts them), so a total field is undecodable. That
  Nothing is a fact about existing data, not a design retreat, and it renders the

- IssueEnhancement's 12 sites keep their local helper: each has a distinct
  per-type fallback string, so converting them needs a Nothing arm reconstructing
  each fallback from issueType — more code, and the consequence there is a
  degraded LLM prompt, not data loss.

Doctests pin the property this exists for: valid JSON for one payload type, read
under a different tag, is rejected rather than coerced — round-tripped through the
real encoder rather than a hand-written literal. My first attempt at those
examples asserted a one-field object would parse as QueryAlertData (7 required
fields) and failed; the corrected form is stronger than what I first wrote.

feat(errors): distil merged groups into masks that run at ingest

Phase 4. The verdict is expensive and arrives after the notification; the rule it
implies is free and arrives before it. Mirrors promoteConfirmedIdRules on the
endpoint side, including the shape of its safety test.

A mask is a literal prefix and suffix around a part that varies — `SB-{hex} not
processing` becomes prefix "SB-", suffix " not processing". Anchored at BOTH ends,
minimum three characters each, because an unanchored mask is a wildcard and a
wildcard merges everything eventually. Scoped to (project, error_type): a mask
learned from one project's order ids has no authority over another's.

**Masks move the shape and never the fingerprint.** That is why `shapeWithMasks`
is a separate function rather than a parameter on computeErrorHashes. A mask that
changed `narrow` would re-key every pattern it touches and mint new issues for
errors we already know about — the same "a rename is a new hash" trap the endpoint
work hit. Moving only the shape is additive: grouping gets coarser, issue identity
stays put. A doctest pins that with no masks the two agree, because a divergence
would not fail, it would quietly stop the ingest gate matching anything.

The safety test is the half that does not trust the model: a candidate is refused
outright if applying it would give one masked form to two shapes the review loop
is currently holding apart — those are either an unanswered question or a judged
"different bugs". Refusals log at attention rather than vanishing.

Promotion re-keys the authorising review AND its members' shape_hash. Without
that the gate resolves arrivals under the post-mask shape, finds a review filed
under the pre-mask one, and the rule silently does nothing. The backfill applies
the same masks for the same reason.

`enableErrorMaskPromotion` defaults OFF, downstream of auto-apply — with nothing
merging there is nothing to promote.

fix(onboarding): make step completion atomic, and share one implementation

Five sites wrote onboarding_steps_completed, using two strategies that are not
equivalent:

- Log.hs and Monitors.hs open-coded an ATOMIC append:
    SET ... = array_append(..., 'x') WHERE id = ? AND NOT ('x' = ANY(...))
- Onboarding.markStepCompleted did a READ-MODIFY-WRITE: take the caller's
  already-read vector, append in Haskell, write the whole array back.

The second has a lost-update race — two requests completing *different* steps
both read the same vector, each appends its own, and the second write clobbers
the first's step. So the helper that existed was the racy one, while the correct
form was duplicated inline in two Pages modules.

delegates and drops its stepsCompleted parameter, so its four call sites no
longer need to have read the project first.

the step, so they need the append folded into that UPDATE rather than a separate
call. Recorded.

refactor(endpoints): use Data.Cache.fetchWithCache instead of our own

Both stats caches hand-rolled the read-through:

  liftIO (Cache.lookup c k) >>= maybe (fetch >>= \fresh -> fresh <$ liftIO (Cache.insert c k fresh)) pure

which is exactly Data.Cache.fetchWithCache, already exported and already a
dependency. Deleted ours.

Worth recording why this did NOT become a shared helper covering all four
call sites. RealUserMonitoring and Containers add an explicit TTL plus a
'is this worth caching' predicate, so the natural generalisation takes a

override' and silently produced unbounded growth on a cache keyed by
user-supplied host and search text. Those two stay hand-rolled.

colour across the app. But a single unnamed aggregate has no identity to encode,

fix(issues): pair the trace id with a timestamp it agrees with, and scope the
logs tab to the trace instead of the page window

Two defects with one root. Every trace lookup on this page pins a +/-5min window
to the timestamp carried alongside the trace id, so the two have to be a matched
pair — and they were not. `updated_at` is bumped by activity that does not set a
new `recent_trace_id`: on the reference issue the recent trace is from 09-02
08:04 while `updated_at` reads 09-04 00:15, and the trace exists nowhere near it.
That mismatch is what made the waterfall report "couldn't load this trace" for an
issue whose trace is present and readable. The pairing is now exact whenever the
recent trace is the first one, which is the common case; when they genuinely
differ the old timestamp is kept, no worse than before.

Separately, the Logs tab scoped a trace-scoped query to the *page's* range rather
than the trace's. A trace happens at an instant, and `virtualTable` fetches on
connect rather than on tab activation, so every runtime-exception page load paid
for it. Measured on the reference issue: the same 14 rows in 0.49s scoped to the
trace, 35.9s over the page's +/-2h. The fallback branch already narrowed this way
and documented why; the trace branch just never did.

Also drops the errM.recentTraceId / traceRef disagreement — traceRef is the trace
the rest of the page shows, it honours First/Recent, and it carries the timestamp
the window needs, which a bare id does not.

The billing page derived its own cycle from the project's billing day, so a
Stripe customer saw usage and an estimate computed over a window their invoice
never covered. For Stripe-billed projects the cycle now comes from the
subscription itself, and past cycles come from the invoices: real charged
amounts, each linked to its hosted invoice. LemonSqueezy, free-tier and
unbilled projects keep the local calculation and make no Stripe call.

Periods are read from items.data[] — API version 2025-03-31.basil moved them
off the subscription, where they now read null. Cycles use each invoice's
top-level period, not its line items: the base-plan line covers the *next*
month (billed in advance) while metered lines cover the past one. Draft, void
and zero-length ($0 trial-opener) invoices are excluded.

Stripe failures fall back to the local cycle and log attention rather than
failing the page.

Rework RUM with grouped errors, audience and per-page vitals

Overview and Performance gain competitor-informed panels driven by data
already ingested: browser errors grouped by signature (normalized message)
with occurrence and session-impact counts, an audience breakdown classifying
user agents into browser/OS/device families, per-page Web Vitals P75s from
the page.url metric attribute, and a per-interval vitals trend colored by
Google's thresholds.

Data fixes: a session's last page is now the latest page view (portable
argmax via MAX(concat(timestamp, '|', path)) FILTER) rather than the
lexicographically largest URL across all browser spans — which on real
traffic was a third-party font URL — and replay-only sessions say
"Recording only" instead of "Unknown page / 0 views · 0 events".

Response times: summary + activity trend are one ROLLUP scan instead of two
full-window scans (the summary alone cost ~7s cold on the demo project), and
the service picker's scan result is held for 15 minutes. All new SQL
verified against both TimescaleDB and TimeFusion.
